citations.quote: The **passive Lorentz boost with parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$** is the linear map $B(\boldsymbol\beta):V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) defined by its action on coordinates: for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$, $$x'^0=\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}),\qquad x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\,(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})\,\boldsymbol\beta-\gamma\,\boldsymbol\beta\,x^0,$$ and for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$, $B(\mathbf 0):=\operatorname{id}_V$. Here $x'$ denotes the coordinates of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ applied to the vector with coordinates $x$, and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the matrix of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is $$\begin{pmatrix}\gamma & -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta & I_3+\dfrac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\,\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix},$$ that is, $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ for $i=1,2,3$, and $B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$ for $i,j=1,2,3$, with the spatial block replaced by $I_3$ when $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$. In the $1+1$ case $\boldsymbol\beta=\beta e_1$ this reads $x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$ and $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$. The vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ is called the **boost parameter**; it is dimensionless and mathematically independent of any unit convention.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$

the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

and for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$, $B(\mathbf 0):=\operatorname{id}_V$.
Here $x'$ denotes the coordinates of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ applied to the
vector with coordinates $x$, and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is
the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the matrix of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}\gamma & -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta & I_3+\dfrac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\,\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix},$$

that is, $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ for
$i=1,2,3$, and
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$
for $i,j=1,2,3$, with the spatial block replaced by
$I_3$ when $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$. In the $1+1$ case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\beta e_1$ this reads
$x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$ and $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$. The vector
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is called the **boost parameter**; it is dimensionless and
mathematically independent of any unit convention.

**Consistency of the definition.** The displayed formulas assign to every
coordinate pair $(x^0,x_{\mathrm{vec}})$ a pair
$(x'^0,x'_{\mathrm{vec}})$; writing the result as the matrix product above and
using that $\mathbb R^4$ is identified with coordinates through
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] (see
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), the map
$v\mapsto E(M(E^{-1}(v)))$ is the unique linear map with that matrix. The case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ is declared separately because the expression
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ is undefined there. That the two cases fit
together is the limit computation recorded next.

**The limit as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$.** For
$\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$ the identity
$\gamma^2-1=|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\gamma^2$ gives

$$\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\gamma+1}.$$

Since $|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\le3/4$ forces $1\le\gamma\le2$, the bounds
$|\beta_i|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|$ and $|\beta_i\beta_j|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$
(from the Euclidean norm convention, [[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]])
show that $\gamma\to1$ as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$; here continuity of
the positive-base power at fixed exponent $-1/2$ is
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], with real and rational powers
identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. Hence
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\to1/2$, so
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac12\beta_i\beta_j+o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)\to I$ entrywise, without a hidden division by zero.
Here $o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ denotes a remainder whose ratio to
$|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ tends to $0$ through nonzero parameters: the ratio
of each spatial remainder is bounded by
$|\gamma^2/(\gamma+1)-1/2|\to0$. The time-space entries obey
$|\gamma\beta_i|\le2|\boldsymbol\beta|\to0$, and the time-time entry tends to
$1$ by $\gamma\to1$. The
definition asserts no Lorentz property: that $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ is proved in
[[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], and its collinear
composition law in
[[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]. The physical
reading of $c\boldsymbol\beta$ as a relative velocity is not part of this
definition ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) and let
$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be its spatial three-space with
$\delta$ the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Then $\delta$ is a
positive-definite symmetric bilinear form, $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is
$\delta$-orthonormal, and $S=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\}$.

A **spatial rotation of the frame** is a linear map $R:V\to V$
([[def-linear-map]]) such that

1. $R(e_0)=e_0$;
2. $R(S)\subseteq S$, so that the restriction $R|_S$ is an endomorphism of
   $S$;
3. $\delta(Rw,Rz)=\delta(w,z)$ for all $w,z\in S$; and
4. the restriction $R|_S$ has determinant $+1$ computed in the ordered basis
   $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]).

Condition 3 makes $R|_S$ injective, since $Rw=0$ with $w\in S$ forces
$\delta(w,w)=\delta(Rw,Rw)=0$ and hence $w=0$ by positive definiteness;
$S$ being finite-dimensional, $R|_S$ is then an automorphism of $S$, so in
fact $R(S)=S$. The extension of such an $R|_S$ by $R(e_0)=e_0$ is also
written $R$ and called a spatial rotation of the frame.

**Matrix form and the group $SO(3)$.** Via the $\delta$-orthonormal basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, a linear map of $V$ fixing $e_0$ and preserving $S$
corresponds to the block matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1,A)$ with
$A\in M_3(\mathbb R)$; under this correspondence the maps of conditions 1-4
are exactly those with

$$A^{T}A=I_3\qquad\text{and}\qquad\det A=+1 .$$

Indeed, the matrix of the adjoint of an endomorphism of the inner product
space $(S,\delta)$ in a $\delta$-orthonormal basis is the transpose of its
matrix ([[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]]), and an
endomorphism of a finite-dimensional inner product space preserves the inner
product exactly when $T^{*}T=I$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-isometry-characterisations]],
[[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]]). Writing
$SO(3):=\{A\in M_3(\mathbb R):A^{T}A=I_3,\ \det A=+1\}$, the orthogonal
operators on $S$ form a group and each of them has determinant $\pm1$
([[cor-orthogonal-and-unitary-operators-form-groups-and-have-unit-determinant-modulus]]),
and $\det(S_1S_2)=\det(S_1)\det(S_2)$ for composable endomorphisms
([[thm-operator-determinant-is-multiplicative]]); hence the determinant-one
part is a subgroup, the spatial rotations of the frame form a subgroup of the
general linear group of $V$, that is, of the group of invertible linear maps
$V\to V$ under composition
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]), and the map
$R\mapsto A(R)$ sending a rotation to
the matrix of $R|_S$ in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is a group isomorphism onto
$SO(3)$. The determinant in condition 4 is independent of the ordered basis of $S$
([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]). Thus, for fixed $\eta$, the
rotation subgroup depends only on the time axis $e_0$: it fixes $e_0$ and
acts on $S=e_0^\perp$ by determinant-one $\delta$-isometries. Changing the
origin or the spatial orthonormal basis while retaining $e_0$ leaves this
subgroup unchanged; changing $e_0$ can change which maps are spatial rotations.
No claim is made here that spatial rotations are Lorentz maps; that is proved
in [[lem-boost-rotation-factorization]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a, b > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, with
rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]]. Then:

1. $a^{r} > 0$.
2. $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$.
3. $(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$; in particular $\big(ab\big)^{1/N} = a^{1/N} b^{1/N}$ for every natural $N \ge 1$.
4. $a^{-r} = \big(a^{r}\big)^{-1} = 1/a^{r}$.
5. $\big(a^{r}\big)^{s} = a^{rs}$.

Claims 2 and 3 persist in the supplementary case of [[def-rational-power]]: for
$a, b \ge 0$ and rationals $r, s > 0$ ([[def-rat-order]]) one still has
$(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$ and $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$. The two identities degenerate
differently, and it is worth saying how. In the product identity, a zero base on
either side makes both sides $0$. In the addition identity only the base $a$
occurs, so it degenerates only when $a = 0$, and then both sides are $0$; when
$a > 0$ that identity holds with no hypothesis on $b$ at all.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

A real $x$ is **positive** when it has a representative $(a_n)$ together
with a rational $\delta > 0$ and an index $N$ such that $a_n > \delta$
for all $n \ge N$. Define

$$x \le y \iff x = y \;\text{ or }\; y - x \text{ is positive},$$

and $|x| = x$ if $x \ge 0$, $|x| = -x$ otherwise.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

derivations.claim: Let $P:=\operatorname{span}(e_0,e)$ and $P^{\perp}:=\{y\in S:\delta(e,y)=0\}$. By

By the product rule [L5], the $2\times2$ blocks of $B_1B_2$ multiply to $\begin{pmatrix}\gamma_1&-\gamma_1\beta_1\\ -\gamma_1\beta_1&\gamma_1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}\gamma_2&-\gamma_2\beta_2\\ -\gamma_2\beta_2&\gamma_2\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}\gamma_1\gamma_2(1+\beta_1\beta_2)&-\gamma_1\gamma_2(\beta_1+\beta_2)\\ -\gamma_1\gamma_2(\beta_1+\beta_2)&\gamma_1\gamma_2(1+\beta_1\beta_2)\end{pmatrix}$, because the $(0,0)$ entry is $\gamma_1\gamma_2+\gamma_1\beta_1\gamma_2\beta_2$ and the $(0,1)$ entry is $-\gamma_1\gamma_2\beta_2-\gamma_1\beta_1\gamma_2$, the other two entries being the same by symmetry; the $P^{\perp}$ block of $B_1B_2$ is the identity. Since $|\beta_1\beta_2|=|\beta_1|\,|\beta_2|<1\cdot1=1$ by [L7], [L6] gives $-1<\beta_1\beta_2$, hence $1+\beta_1\beta_2>0$; the scalar $\gamma_1\gamma_2(1+\beta_1\beta_2)$ is the product of the positive numbers $\gamma_1,\gamma_2,1+\beta_1\beta_2$ and is therefore positive, so the block may be factored by it.

Define $\beta:=(\beta_1+\beta_2)/(1+\beta_1\beta_2)$. Expanding the numerator of $1-\beta^2$ with the common denominator $(1+\beta_1\beta_2)^2$ gives $1-\beta^2=\frac{(1+\beta_1\beta_2)^2-(\beta_1+\beta_2)^2}{(1+\beta_1\beta_2)^2} =\frac{(1-\beta_1^2)(1-\beta_2^2)}{(1+\beta_1\beta_2)^2} =\frac{1}{\gamma_1^2\gamma_2^2(1+\beta_1\beta_2)^2}$, where the last step uses $\gamma_i^2(1-\beta_i^2)=1$ from [L4]. The right-hand side is positive, so $1-\beta^2>0$ and $|\beta|<1$; moreover $\gamma(\beta)^2=1/(1-\beta^2)=\gamma_1^2\gamma_2^2(1+\beta_1\beta_2)^2$ by [L4], and $\gamma(\beta)$ and $\gamma_1\gamma_2(1+\beta_1\beta_2)$ are both positive, so their equal squares force them to be equal (a positive real has exactly one positive square root); consequently $\gamma(\beta)\beta=\gamma_1\gamma_2(\beta_1+\beta_2)$. For the positivity of the numerator in the second display, note that $|\beta_i|<1=|1|$, so [L8] gives $\beta_i^2<1$, hence $1-\beta_i^2>0$ and, by [L6], $(1-\beta_1^2)(1-\beta_2^2)>0$; together with $(1+\beta_1\beta_2)^2>0$ from [L6] this gives $1-\beta^2>0$ and, by [L8] applied to $\beta^2<1$, the bound $|\beta|<1$.

Substituting the two displays of step 3.1 into the product of step 2.1 and comparing with the block action of $B(\beta e)$ established in step 1.1 (including $\beta=0$, when the block is $I_2$) gives that $B_1B_2$ and $B(\beta e)$ have the same action on $P$ in $(e_0,e)$, namely the $2\times2$ matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\gamma(\beta)&-\gamma(\beta)\beta\\ -\gamma(\beta)\beta&\gamma(\beta)\end{pmatrix}$ and both fix $P^{\perp}$ pointwise; since $V=P\oplus P^{\perp}$,

Replacing $\beta_2$ by $-\beta_2$ in steps 2.1 and 3.1 (the hypothesis $|-\beta_2|<1$ holds and $|\beta_1\beta_2|<1$ gives $1-\beta_1\beta_2>0$ by [L6], [L7]) gives the product $\gamma_1\gamma_2(1-\beta_1\beta_2) \begin{pmatrix}1&-\frac{\beta_1-\beta_2}{1-\beta_1\beta_2}\\ -\frac{\beta_1-\beta_2}{1-\beta_1\beta_2}&1\end{pmatrix}$, the identity on $P^{\perp}$, and the identity $(1-\beta_1^2)(1-\beta_2^2)=(1-\beta_1\beta_2)^2\bigl(1-\bigl(\frac{\beta_1-\beta_2}{1-\beta_1\beta_2}\bigr)^2\bigr)$; hence $\beta':=\frac{\beta_1-\beta_2}{1-\beta_1\beta_2}$ satisfies $|\beta'|<1$ and, by the same comparison as step 4.1, $B(\beta_1e)B(-\beta_2e)=B(\beta'e)$.

The displays of steps 3.1 and 4.1 are symmetric under the exchange of $(\beta_1,\gamma_1)$ with $(\beta_2,\gamma_2)$: the scalar $\beta$ and the factor $\gamma_1\gamma_2(1+\beta_1\beta_2)$ are unchanged by that exchange. Applying the same computation with the roles of $B_1$ and $B_2$ interchanged therefore gives $B(\beta_2e)B(\beta_1e)=B(\beta e)=B(\beta_1e)B(\beta_2e)$: the two collinear boosts commute.

Step 4.1 proves the composition law and the bound $|\beta|<1$ for equal directions, step 5.1 proves the opposite-sign composition law, and step 5.2 proves commutativity; every composition of two boosts in the common direction $e$ therefore has parameter in $(-1,1)$ and never leaves the open interval. This proves every clause of the statement.

boundaries.reason: The sums defining J(a), the coordinate inner product and norm run over exactly i=1,2,3. The product in proof step 2.1 contracts the two coordinates of the fixed plane span(e_0,e); it is a 2 by 2 block, not a variable-size family. The frame has four basis vectors and the unit e is nonzero, so neither index range can be empty under the hypotheses.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 2.1-3.1 apply the rational composition formula to all parameter pairs, including $\beta_i=0$, where the formula returns the other parameter; $1+\beta_1\beta_2>0$ prevents division by zero.
Step 3.1 computes $\gamma(\beta)^2=1/(1-\beta^2)$ and $\gamma(\beta)\beta=\gamma_1\gamma_2(\beta_1+\beta_2)$, including the equal-parameter case; step 5.1 treats the opposite-sign composition.

Step 3.1 shows $(1-\beta_1^2)(1-\beta_2^2)>0$ so the composed denominator never degenerates, and the factors of the matrix product are nonzero; step 1.1 splits off the degenerate perpendicular complement correctly.
Steps 3.1 and 5.1 prove the composed parameter always satisfies $|\beta|<1$ strictly, so the open interval is preserved and its endpoints are never attained.

boundaries.reason: The proof compares explicit matrices in a fixed ordered basis; no selection from a family is made.
The lemma asserts composition laws and inequalities, not a biconditional.
The lemma contains no converse implication to check.

risk_review.notes: All seven steps checked: common-axis block multiplication gives numerator beta1+beta2 and strictly positive denominator 1+beta1 beta2. The identity 1-beta²=(1-beta1²)(1-beta2²)/(1+beta1 beta2)² proves subunit output and the positive gamma branch. Zero inputs and opposite inputs (zero output) use B(0)=I; the sign-reversed formula and commutativity follow by the same computation. The rational law generally differs from the sum, with legitimate equality exceptions. No endpoint ±1 or physical velocity premise is used.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

$$\exp:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(0,\infty)$$
is a bijection.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a, b > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, with
rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]]. Then:

1. $a^{r} > 0$.
2. $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$.
3. $(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$; in particular $\big(ab\big)^{1/N} = a^{1/N} b^{1/N}$ for every natural $N \ge 1$.
4. $a^{-r} = \big(a^{r}\big)^{-1} = 1/a^{r}$.
5. $\big(a^{r}\big)^{s} = a^{rs}$.

Claims 2 and 3 persist in the supplementary case of [[def-rational-power]]: for
$a, b \ge 0$ and rationals $r, s > 0$ ([[def-rat-order]]) one still has
$(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$ and $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$. The two identities degenerate
differently, and it is worth saying how. In the product identity, a zero base on
either side makes both sides $0$. In the addition identity only the base $a$
occurs, so it degenerates only when $a = 0$, and then both sides are $0$; when
$a > 0$ that identity holds with no hypothesis on $b$ at all.

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be its coordinates, so that a vector is written
$x=x^0e_0+x^1e_1+x^2e_2+x^3e_3$ and the spatial part is the coordinate
column $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ with its standard
Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

For $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$, where
$|\boldsymbol\beta|$ is the Euclidean norm, set

$$\gamma(\boldsymbol\beta):=(1-|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)^{-1/2}\ \ge 1,$$

with equality exactly for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ and strict inequality
for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$; here the power is the rational power
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). The **passive Lorentz
boost with parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$** is the linear map
$B(\boldsymbol\beta):V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) defined by its action on
coordinates: for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$,

$$x'^0=\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}),\qquad x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\,(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})\,\boldsymbol\beta-\gamma\,\boldsymbol\beta\,x^0,$$

and for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$, $B(\mathbf 0):=\operatorname{id}_V$.
Here $x'$ denotes the coordinates of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ applied to the
vector with coordinates $x$, and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is
the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the matrix of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}\gamma & -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta & I_3+\dfrac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\,\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix},$$

that is, $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ for
$i=1,2,3$, and
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$
for $i,j=1,2,3$, with the spatial block replaced by
$I_3$ when $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$. In the $1+1$ case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\beta e_1$ this reads
$x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$ and $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$. The vector
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is called the **boost parameter**; it is dimensionless and
mathematically independent of any unit convention.

**Consistency of the definition.** The displayed formulas assign to every
coordinate pair $(x^0,x_{\mathrm{vec}})$ a pair
$(x'^0,x'_{\mathrm{vec}})$; writing the result as the matrix product above and
using that $\mathbb R^4$ is identified with coordinates through
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] (see
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), the map
$v\mapsto E(M(E^{-1}(v)))$ is the unique linear map with that matrix. The case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ is declared separately because the expression
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ is undefined there. That the two cases fit
together is the limit computation recorded next.

**The limit as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$.** For
$\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$ the identity
$\gamma^2-1=|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\gamma^2$ gives

$$\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\gamma+1}.$$

Since $|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\le3/4$ forces $1\le\gamma\le2$, the bounds
$|\beta_i|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|$ and $|\beta_i\beta_j|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$
(from the Euclidean norm convention, [[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]])
show that $\gamma\to1$ as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$; here continuity of
the positive-base power at fixed exponent $-1/2$ is
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], with real and rational powers
identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. Hence
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\to1/2$, so
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac12\beta_i\beta_j+o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)\to I$ entrywise, without a hidden division by zero.
Here $o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ denotes a remainder whose ratio to
$|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ tends to $0$ through nonzero parameters: the ratio
of each spatial remainder is bounded by
$|\gamma^2/(\gamma+1)-1/2|\to0$. The time-space entries obey
$|\gamma\beta_i|\le2|\boldsymbol\beta|\to0$, and the time-time entry tends to
$1$ by $\gamma\to1$. The
definition asserts no Lorentz property: that $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ is proved in
[[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], and its collinear
composition law in
[[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]. The physical
reading of $c\boldsymbol\beta$ as a relative velocity is not part of this
definition ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

Let $S=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be the spatial three-space of a frame
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with its Euclidean structure $\delta$
([[def-spatial-rotation-of-an-inertial-frame]]), and let $e\in S$ be a unit
vector, $\delta(e,e)=1$. Define $J:\mathbb R^3\to S$ by
$J(a):=\sum_{i=1}^3a_i e_i$, where $a_i:=a(i-1)$ relabels the coordinates
$0,1,2$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Let $n:=J^{-1}(e)$; then
$|n|=1$, since $\delta(J(a),J(b))=a\cdot b$ by orthonormality.
For $t\in(-1,1)$, the notation $B(te)$ means $B(tn)$, whose parameter
belongs to $\mathbb R^3$, while $e$ belongs to $V$.
Let $\beta_1,\beta_2\in(-1,1)$ be real parameters and
let $B(\beta_1e)$ and $B(\beta_2e)$ be the corresponding passive boosts
([[def-lorentz-boost]]). Then

$$B(\beta_1e)\,B(\beta_2e)=B(\beta e),\qquad \beta:=\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2},$$

and $|\beta|<1$. In particular the two collinear boosts commute,
$B(\beta_1e)B(\beta_2e)=B(\beta_2e)B(\beta_1e)$, and

$$B(\beta_1e)\,B(-\beta_2e)=B\!\left(\frac{\beta_1-\beta_2}{1-\beta_1\beta_2}\,e\right).$$

The composed parameter $\beta$ is the displayed rational expression, which
generally differs from $\beta_1+\beta_2$; this algebraic law is conventionally
called velocity addition. In particular,
no composition of two boosts in a common direction leaves the open interval
$(-1,1)$: the composed parameter always satisfies $|\beta|<1$.

Let $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ be the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] in an
inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. For every
$\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the following
hold.

(i) $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map:
$\eta(B(\boldsymbol\beta)v,B(\boldsymbol\beta)w)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$,
$\det B(\boldsymbol\beta)=+1$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)(C^+)=C^+$.

(ii) $B(\mathbf 0)$ is the identity, and for every $\boldsymbol\beta$ the image
of the frame vector $e_0$ is
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)e_0=\gamma\,(e_0-\beta_1e_1-\beta_2e_2-\beta_3e_3)$, so
the map $\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is injective and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ fixes $0_V$; moreover every vector $y$ with
coordinates $(0,y_{\mathrm{vec}})$ and
$\boldsymbol\beta\cdot y_{\mathrm{vec}}=0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)y=y$.

(iii) $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)B(\boldsymbol\beta)
=B(\boldsymbol\beta)B(-\boldsymbol\beta)=\operatorname{id}_V$; in particular
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is invertible with
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and
$B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ are inverse bijections of $V$.

(iv) If $u$ is a future timelike unit vector with coordinates
$(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$, so that $\eta(u,u)=-1$, $u^0>0$ and
$|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|<u^0$, then the boost with parameter
$\boldsymbol\beta:=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)u=e_0$.

(v) If a vector $x$ has $x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$, then the first coordinate of
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)x$ is $\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})>0$;
if $x^0<-|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ then that first coordinate is negative. In
particular $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ maps the future open cone
$\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ into itself.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

derivations.claim: For every real $x$, set $a_x:=\exp(x)$. By [L2] with $y=-x$, $a_xa_{-x}=\exp(0)$; applying [L2] with $x=y=0$ gives $\exp(0)=\exp(0)^2$, and $\exp(0)\neq0$ because the codomain of $\exp$ is $(0,\infty)$ by [L1], so $\exp(0)=1$ and $a_{-x}=a_x^{-1}$. Also $a_x=(a_{x/2})^2>0$ because $a_{x/2}>0$ by [L1]. Consequently $\cosh^2(r)-\sinh^2(r)=\frac{(a_r+a_{-r})^2-(a_r-a_{-r})^2}{4}=a_ra_{-r}=1$ for every $r$, and $\cosh(r)=\frac{a_r+a_r^{-1}}2>0$.

Multiplying numerator and denominator by $a_r$ gives $\tanh(r)=\frac{a_r-a_r^{-1}}{a_r+a_r^{-1}}=\frac{a_r^2-1}{a_r^2+1}=\frac{e^{2r}-1}{e^{2r}+1}$ by [L2], since $e^{2r}=a_r^2$. Since $e^{2r}>0$, the numerator $e^{2r}-1$ is strictly smaller in absolute value than the denominator $e^{2r}+1$, so $-1<\tanh(r)<1$; thus $\tanh$ maps $\mathbb R$ into $(-1,1)$. For $0<u<v$ one computes $\frac{v-1}{v+1}-\frac{u-1}{u+1}=\frac{(v-1)(u+1)-(u-1)(v+1)}{(v+1)(u+1)}=\frac{2(v-u)}{(v+1)(u+1)}>0$, so $u\mapsto\frac{u-1}{u+1}$ is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$; since $r\mapsto e^{2r}=\exp(2r)$ is strictly increasing by [L1], the composition $\tanh$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $\beta\in(-1,1)$ and put $u:=\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}>0$, the denominator being positive. By [L1] there is a real $t$ with $e^t=u$; put $s:=t/2$, so $e^{2s}=(e^s)^2=e^t=u$ by [L2]. Then step 1.2 gives $\tanh(s)=\frac{u-1}{u+1}=\frac{(1+\beta)-(1-\beta)}{(1+\beta)+(1-\beta)}=\frac{2\beta}{2}=\beta$. Hence $\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is surjective, and with step 1.2 it is a strictly increasing bijection; its inverse $\tanh^{-1}:(-1,1)\to\mathbb R$ is strictly increasing and onto.

For $r,s\in\mathbb R$ put $\beta_1:=\tanh(r)$ and $\beta_2:=\tanh(s)$. Both lie in $(-1,1)$, so $1+\beta_1\beta_2>0$. Writing $u:=e^{2r}$, $v:=e^{2s}$, step 1.2 gives $\beta_1=(u-1)/(u+1)$ and $\beta_2=(v-1)/(v+1)$, while [L2] gives $e^{2(r+s)}=uv$. Hence $\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2}=\frac{(u-1)(v+1)+(v-1)(u+1)}{(u+1)(v+1)+(u-1)(v-1)}=\frac{2uv-2}{2uv+2}=\tanh(r+s)$. This checks the parameter identity of the collinear composition law; the map equality will follow from the boost plane matrices.

For $\beta\in(-1,1)$, put $q:=\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}>0$ and $r:=r(\beta)=\tfrac12\log q$, so $2r=\log q$. By [L3], $e^{2r}=\exp(\log q)=q$. Then step 1.2 gives $\tanh(r(\beta))=\frac{q-1}{q+1}=\frac{(1+\beta)-(1-\beta)}{(1+\beta)+(1-\beta)}=\beta$. Thus $\tanh\circ r=\operatorname{id}_{(-1,1)}$; composing with the bijection $\tanh$ of step 2.1 gives $r=\tanh^{-1}$, so $r$ is a strictly increasing bijection of $(-1,1)$ onto $\mathbb R$, and in particular $\beta=\tanh(r(\beta))$ for every $\beta$.

Let $r\in\mathbb R$ and put $\beta:=\tanh(r)\in(-1,1)$, so that $r=r(\beta)$ by step 3.1. By step 1.1, $1-\tanh(r)^2=\frac{\cosh^2r-\sinh^2r}{\cosh^2r}=\cosh(r)^{-2}$; since $\cosh(r)>0$ by step 1.1, the rational power laws [L4] give $(1-\tanh(r)^2)^{-1/2}=(\cosh(r)^{-2})^{-1/2}=\cosh(r)$. Multiplying the definition $\tanh r=\sinh r/\cosh r$ by $\cosh r$ gives $\sinh(r)=\tanh(r)\cosh(r)=\beta\gamma(\beta)$, because $\gamma(\beta)=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}=(1-\tanh(r)^2)^{-1/2}=\cosh(r)$ by [L5].

Fix $e$ and its column $n$, and define $J(a):=\sum_{i=1}^3 a_i e_i$ for $a\in\mathbb R^3$. By [L8], $J(n)=e$ and $\eta(J(a),J(d))=a\cdot d$. Write $x=x^0e_0+se+y$ with $s:=n\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$, $y_{\mathrm{vec}}:=x_{\mathrm{vec}}-sn$, and $y:=J(y_{\mathrm{vec}})$; then $n\cdot y_{\mathrm{vec}}=\eta(e,y)=0$. Set $\beta:=\tanh(r)$ and $\boldsymbol\beta:=\beta n\in\mathbb R^3$, so $|\boldsymbol\beta|=|\beta|<1$ and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}=\beta s$. If $\beta=0$, step 4.1 gives $\cosh r=1$, $\sinh r=0$, and [L5] gives $B(0)=I$. If $\beta\ne0$, [L5] gives $(B(\beta n)x)^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta s)$ and $(B(\beta n)x)_{\mathrm{vec}}=sn+y_{\mathrm{vec}}+(\gamma-1)sn-\gamma\beta x^0n=(\cosh r\,s-\sinh r\,x^0)n+y_{\mathrm{vec}}$ by step 4.1. Thus in both cases the action in directions $(e_0,e)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}\cosh r&-\sinh r\\-\sinh r&\cosh r\end{pmatrix}$, with the identity on the Lorentz-orthogonal complement of their plane, namely $\{J(a):n\cdot a=0\}$.

By [L2] and the exponential definitions, expansion gives $\cosh(r+s)=\cosh r\cosh s+\sinh r\sinh s$ and $\sinh(r+s)=\sinh r\cosh s+\cosh r\sinh s$. The product of the two plane matrices from step 5.1 therefore has diagonal entries $\cosh(r+s)$ and off-diagonal entries $-\sinh(r+s)$; each map is the identity on the same transverse space. The direct-sum decomposition in step 5.1 then gives $B(\tanh(r)e)B(\tanh(s)e)=B(\tanh(r+s)e)$ on all of $V$, including zero rapidities. Together with step 2.2 this proves the collinear composition law stated in [L6], with additive rapidity.

Step 3.1 proves that $r$ is a strictly increasing bijection of $(-1,1)$ onto $\mathbb R$ with $\beta=\tanh(r(\beta))$; step 1.1 gives $\cosh^2-\sinh^2=1$; step 4.1 gives $(1-\tanh^2r)^{-1/2}=\cosh r$ and $\sinh r=\tanh r\cosh r=\beta\gamma(\beta)$; step 5.1 gives the matrix display and the identity on the perpendicular complement; and step 6.1 gives the addition of rapidities. This proves every clause of the statement; the characterisation $B(\tanh r e)^{-1}=B(-\tanh r e)$ used implicitly is [L7].

boundaries.evidence: The Statement fixes a four-vector frame and a unit spatial direction with three coordinates. Step 5.1 sums over i=1,2,3, a nonempty fixed index set. Fact L1 uses the exponential series indexed by n>=0, whose index set contains 0 and whose zeroth term is 1. Steps 1.1-3.1 use positive exponential values on all of R and parameters in (-1,1), which contains 0; no empty indexed sum is substituted for either series or spatial expansion.
Step 5.1 explicitly handles beta=0 using B(0)=id, cosh r=1 and sinh r=0; step 6.1 multiplies the plane matrices for all real r,s, including r=0 or s=0.
Step 2.1 proves the map $r$ is a bijection, hence each $\beta$ has a unique rapidity; step 5.1 computes the $2\times2$ block with $\det=1$ and the identity on the perpendicular complement.
Step 1.1 shows $\cosh r>0$ is never zero; step 5.1 fixes the whole perpendicular complement, so the direction $e$ produces no degenerate case.
Step 2.1 shows $\tanh$ maps onto $(-1,1)$ without attaining $\pm1$; the boundary values are limits, not values, and steps 1.2 and 3.1 work on the open interval.

boundaries.reason: The inverse of the explicit bijection is constructed by the formula $r(\beta)=\tfrac12\log\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}$; no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 2.1-3.1 prove $\beta=\tanh(r(\beta))$ for every $\beta\in(-1,1)$, the forward direction.
Step 2.1 proves every $r\in\mathbb R$ is the exponential-type parameter $\tanh r$ of a boost and step 3.1 gives $\tanh\circ r=\mathrm{id}$, supplying the converse.

risk_review.notes: All eight steps checked: positive exponential and inverse logarithm give tanh(r)=(exp(2r)-1)/(exp(2r)+1), a strictly increasing bijection onto (-1,1). Solving yields r(beta)=half log((1+beta)/(1-beta)); cosh is positive and gamma=cosh, beta gamma=sinh. Zero beta has r=0 and identity block before quotient cancellation. Exponential addition yields the collinear rational composition and additive rapidity. Endpoints are excluded and no infinite logarithm is taken.
