citations.quote:
Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with a chosen time
orientation $C^+$, and let $L:V\to V$ be a linear map with
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]). Then:

(i) $L$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$; for every ordered $\eta$-orthonormal
basis the matrix $M$ of $L$ satisfies $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ with
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and conversely every invertible matrix
$M$ with $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ is the matrix of a linear Lorentz map in that
basis.

(ii) $\det L=\pm1$. The composition of two Lorentz maps is a Lorentz map, the
identity is a Lorentz map, and the inverse of a Lorentz map is a Lorentz map;
the sets $SO(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):\det L=1\}$,
$O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):L(C^+)=C^+\}$ and
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)=SO(V,\eta)\cap O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta)$ are subgroups of
$O(V,\eta)$, which itself is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL(V)$.

(iii) $\eta(Lv,Lv)=\eta(v,v)$ for all $v\in V$; hence $L$ preserves the causal
character of every nonzero vector (timelike, null or spacelike) and maps the
set of null vectors onto itself. If $L$ is proper, then the oriented volume
form is preserved:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,\dots,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]); if
$\det L=-1$ the two sides differ by the sign $-1$.

(iv) $L(C^+)$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$ of the timelike set, so
exactly one of $L(C^+)=C^+$ and $L(C^+)=C^-$ holds; $L$ is orthochronous in
the first case and non-orthochronous in the second, and $L(C^+)=C^+$ holds if
and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

(v) The affine Lorentz maps of
[[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]] form a group under composition: the
composition and the inverse of affine Lorentz maps are affine Lorentz maps,
and every affine Lorentz map is a bijection of $A$.

An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with the following data. In this notation $V$ includes its
specified orientation; forgetting that orientation gives only the underlying
real vector space, not the full datum $V$ of the model.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ be one inertial chart. Give $A$ the **transported topology**
in which a set $U\subseteq A$ is open exactly when $x(U)$ is open in
$\mathbb R^4$; this is the unique topology making $x$ a homeomorphism onto
$\mathbb R^4$. Then:

1. $A$ is a Hausdorff, second-countable topological $4$-manifold.
2. The one-chart family $\{(A,x)\}$ is a smooth atlas, so $A$ is a smooth
   $4$-manifold, and $x$ is a diffeomorphism onto $\mathbb R^4$ carrying its
   standard smooth structure.
3. Every affine chart of $A$, that is, every map $y(p)=Mx(p)+b$ with $M$ an
   invertible $4\times4$ real matrix and $b\in\mathbb R^4$, and in particular
   every inertial chart, belongs to the same smooth structure, and its
   transition with $x$ is the smooth diffeomorphism $u\mapsto Mu+b$ of
   $\mathbb R^4$, with inverse $u\mapsto M^{-1}(u-b)$.
4. The transported topology and the smooth structure do not depend on the choice
   of the initial inertial chart $x$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space with
the smooth structure of [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]], and
let $p\in A$. A smooth germ at $p$ is the equivalence class of a smooth real function on an
open neighbourhood of $p$, where representatives agreeing on a smaller
neighbourhood are equivalent ([[def-germ-of-a-smooth-function-at-a-point]]).
For such a germ $[f]$ define

$$\Phi_p(v)([f]):=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}f(p+tv),\qquad v\in V .$$

Then $\Phi_p:V\to T_pA$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$ onto the tangent space
$T_pA$; in particular $T_pA$ is canonically identified with $V$, independently
of any chart. If $x$ is an inertial chart and
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$, then the coordinate derivations satisfy
$\Phi_p(v)=\sum_av^a\partial_a|_p$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)$ exists for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$ and equals $Df(a)v$. In particular $\partial_jf(a)=Df(a)e_j$, and the matrix of $Df(a)$ is $Jf(a)$.
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

If $f,g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ are totally differentiable at $a$ and $c\in\mathbb R$, then $f+g$ and $cf$ are totally differentiable at $a$, with

$$D(f+g)(a)=Df(a)+Dg(a),\qquad D(cf)(a)=cDf(a).$$
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open. If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at every point and $Df(z)=0$ for every $z\in U$, then $f$ is constant on $U$.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

Let $V$ be a $4$-dimensional real vector space ([[def-vector-space]],
[[def-dimension]]). A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

1. $\eta$ is nondegenerate: both radicals
   $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{u:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\}$ and
   $\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{v:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}$ are
   $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]);
   and
2. $\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

The inertia of a symmetric bilinear form is the triple $(p,q,r)$ of numbers of
positive, negative and zero diagonal entries of any diagonalizing basis, and it
is independent of the diagonalizing basis by Sylvester's law of inertia
([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); hence clause 2
is a property of $\eta$ itself and not of a chosen basis. The **associated
quadratic form** of $\eta$ is

$$q(v):=\eta(v,v),\qquad v\in V .$$

A **Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** is a pair $(V,\eta)$
consisting of a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ and a Lorentz form $\eta$
on $V$; the name records that the diagonal normal form of $\eta$ has one
negative entry followed by three positive entries. No positive-definite
structure on $V$ is assumed or implied by this definition, and $q$ takes both
negative and positive values on nonzero vectors: a basis in which
$\eta$ is diagonal with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$ exists by clause 2, and on
its first vector $q$ is $-1$, while on each of the other three it is $+1$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) that is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F V = n$ ([[def-dimension]]), and let $U$ be a
linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Then

1. $U$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and $\dim_F U \le n$;
2. $\dim_F U = n$ **if and only if** $U = V$;
3. **Extension, with no choice principle.** Every linearly independent
   $A_0 \subseteq U$ is contained in a basis of $U$: there is a basis $B$ of $U$
   with $A_0 \subseteq B \subseteq U$. Claim 1 is the case $A_0 = \varnothing$.
   Since $V$ is itself a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), claim 3
   applies with $V$ in place of $U$, and hence to **any** finite-dimensional
   vector space over $F$ in place of the pair $(V, U)$.

**Nothing above uses a choice principle**, and claim 3 in particular is the
finite-dimensional substitute for the Zorn-based extension theorem stated earlier
on this page. In finite dimension the extension terminates on its own, because
[[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] bounds the size
of an independent set and [[thm-well-ordering-principle]] then supplies a largest
one; no selection is made anywhere.

**Finiteness is essential in claim 2.** Without it the equality case fails: the
companion page exhibits a
proper linear subspace of an infinite-dimensional space whose basis is
equinumerous with a basis of the whole space.

derivations.claim: Put $\Phi:=x\circ F\circ x^{-1}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$, the coordinate expression of $F$ in the chart $x$. By hypothesis and [L5], $\Phi$ is $C^2$ on the open set $\mathbb R^4$; by the chain rule [L12] and the tangent identification [L6], at $u=x(p)$ the total derivative of $\Phi$ is the conjugate $D\Phi_u=E^{-1}\circ dF_p\circ E$ of the total derivative of $F$. Hence for all $u\in\mathbb R^4$ and all $a,b\in\mathbb R^4$, using $\eta(Ec,Ed)=\eta_0(c,d)$ from [L4] and the preservation identity of the Given, $\eta_0(D\Phi_ua,D\Phi_ub)=\eta(dF_p(Ea),dF_p(Eb))=\eta(Ea,Eb)=\eta_0(a,b)$. In particular, if $D\Phi_ua=0$ for some $a$, then $\eta_0(a,b)=\eta_0(D\Phi_ua,D\Phi_ub)=0$ for every $b$; testing $b=e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ gives $a^0=0$ and $a^1=a^2=a^3=0$, so $a=0$ by [L16], and $D\Phi_u$ has trivial kernel; by [L17] it is invertible, so the vectors $D\Phi_ue_0,\dots,D\Phi_ue_3$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^4$.

Conversely, let $G$ be an affine Lorentz map with linear part $\widetilde L$ and $G(p)=G(p_0)+\widetilde L(p-p_0)$. Its coordinate expression in $x$ is $\Phi_G(u)=x(G(x^{-1}(u)))=x(G(p_0))+\widetilde L_x(u-x(p_0))$ with $\widetilde L_x:=E^{-1}\circ\widetilde L\circ E$ a linear map of $\mathbb R^4$, hence a polynomial map of degree at most one and consequently $C^\infty$; its total derivative at every point is the constant $\widetilde L_x$, and for $a,b\in\mathbb R^4$ the Lorentz property of $\widetilde L$ together with [L4] gives $\eta_0(\widetilde L_xa,\widetilde L_xb)=\eta(\widetilde L(Ea),\widetilde L(Eb))=\eta(Ea,Eb)=\eta_0(a,b)$, which under the identification [L6] is exactly the preservation identity $\eta(dG_pv,dG_pw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $p,v,w$.

For $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ define the vector-valued map $A_j:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$ by $A_j(u):=\partial_j\Phi(u)=D\Phi_ue_j$, the equality being [L10]; each $A_j$ is $C^1$ because $\Phi$ is $C^2$. For $i,j,k$ define the real-valued function $C_{ijk}(u):=\eta_0(\partial_iA_j(u),A_k(u))=\eta_0(\partial_i\partial_j\Phi(u),\partial_k\Phi(u))$. The identity of step 1.1, $\eta_0(A_j(u),A_k(u))=\eta_{jk}$ with the constant $\eta_{jk}:=\eta_0(e_j,e_k)$, says that $u\mapsto\eta_0(A_j(u),A_k(u))$ is constant; differentiating it with the product rule for the bilinear form $\eta_0$ (which in coordinates is the displayed polynomial of [L16]) gives $C_{ijk}(u)+C_{ikj}(u)=0$ for all $u$. Clairaut's theorem [L11] applied to the components of the $C^2$ map $\Phi$ gives $\partial_i\partial_j\Phi=\partial_j\partial_i\Phi$ pointwise, hence $C_{ijk}=\eta_0(\partial_j\partial_i\Phi,\partial_k\Phi)=C_{jik}$.

We show $C_{ijk}=0$ for all $i,j,k$. If $i,j,k$ are pairwise distinct, the two relations of step 2.1 give $C_{ijk}=C_{jik}=-C_{jki}=-C_{kji}=C_{kij}=C_{ikj}=-C_{ijk}$, where each equality is an instance of $C_{abc}=C_{bac}$ (first two indices) or $C_{abc}=-C_{acb}$ (last two indices); hence $2C_{ijk}=0$ and $C_{ijk}=0$ in $\mathbb R$. If exactly two of $i,j,k$ coincide, consider the three possible coincidences: $C_{iik}=-C_{iki}$ and $C_{iki}=C_{kii}$ and $C_{kii}=-C_{kii}$, so $C_{kii}=0$, then $C_{iki}=0$, then $C_{iik}=0$; the remaining coincidences are the same three after renaming. If $i=j=k$, then $C_{iii}=-C_{iii}$ by the last-two relation, so $C_{iii}=0$. Thus $C_{ijk}=0$ for every triple.

Fix $i,j$ and $u$, and put $w:=\partial_iA_j(u)\in\mathbb R^4$. By step 3.1, $\eta_0(w,A_k(u))=C_{ijk}(u)=0$ for $k=0,1,2,3$; since $(A_0(u),\dots,A_3(u))$ is a basis of $\mathbb R^4$ by step 1.1, expanding an arbitrary $z\in\mathbb R^4$ in that basis and using bilinearity of $\eta_0$ gives $\eta_0(w,z)=0$ for every $z$, whence $w=0$ by [L16]. Therefore $\partial_iA_j(u)=0$ for all $i,j,u$; equivalently the total derivative $DA_j(u)$, whose matrix is the Jacobian $(\partial_i(A_j)_m(u))$ by [L10], is the zero linear map for every $u$.

By step 4.1 and [L14], applied on the convex open set $\mathbb R^4$ of [L15], each map $A_j:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$ is constant on $\mathbb R^4$: there are vectors $L_j\in\mathbb R^4$ with $A_j(u)=L_j$ for all $u$ and all $j$.

Let $L:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$ be the linear map defined by $Le_j:=L_j$ for $j=0,1,2,3$ ([[def-linear-map]]); it is well defined because $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ is a basis of $\mathbb R^4$. By step 5.1 and step 2.1, $D\Phi_ue_j=A_j(u)=L_j=Le_j$ for all $u$ and all $j$, so the two linear maps $D\Phi_u$ and $L$ agree on a basis and $D\Phi_u=L$ for every $u$. Define $\Psi(u):=\Phi(u)-Lu$; by [L13] $\Psi$ is totally differentiable at every point, and since the linear map $L$ is totally differentiable with $DL(u)=L$ (substituting $L(u+h)-L(u)-Lh=0$ into [L8] verifies the defining limit), [L13] gives $D\Psi(u)=D\Phi_u-L=L-L=0$ for every $u$. Applying [L14] on the convex open set $\mathbb R^4$ again gives a vector $b\in\mathbb R^4$ with $\Psi(u)=b$ for all $u$; hence $\Phi(u)=Lu+b$ for all $u\in\mathbb R^4$.

Evaluating the preservation identity of step 1.1 at $u=0$ and using $D\Phi_0=L$ from step 6.1 gives $\eta_0(La,Lb)=\eta_0(a,b)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R^4$. Define the linear map $\widetilde L:V\to V$ by $\widetilde L:=E\circ L\circ E^{-1}$; for $v=Ea$, $w=Eb$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R^4$, [L4] gives $\eta(\widetilde Lv,\widetilde Lw)=\eta(E(La),E(Lb))=\eta_0(La,Lb)=\eta_0(a,b)=\eta(v,w)$, so $\widetilde L$ is a linear Lorentz map by [L1]. Moreover, for every event $p$ with $u:=x(p)$, step 6.1 and the chart identity $x^{-1}(u)=o+E(u)$ of [L4] give $F(p)=x^{-1}(\Phi(u))=x^{-1}(Lu+b)=o+E(Lu+b)=o+Eb+E(Lu)=F(o)+\widetilde L(E(u))$, and since $x(p)=E^{-1}(p-o)$ this reads $F(p)=F(o)+\widetilde L(p-o)$ for every $p\in A$: $F$ is an affine Lorentz map with linear part $\widetilde L$ and $p_0:=o$.

Step 1.1 sets up the coordinate expression and proves $D\Phi_u$ injective; steps 3.1 through 7.1 construct the constant linear part $\widetilde L$ and prove that it is a linear Lorentz map; step 1.2 is the converse. Hence the $C^2$ isometries of the model are exactly its affine Lorentz maps, and these form a group under composition by [L2] (with every affine Lorentz map being a bijection).

boundaries.evidence: The Statement is nonempty: every affine Lorentz map is a $C^\infty$ instance of a $C^2$ $\eta$-preserving map by the converse clause, which step 8.1 records.
Proof 4.1 proves the second derivative vanishes; Proof 6.1 subtracts the constant linear part and proves the remainder constant. Proof 7.1 uses p−o in V; the event o is not a zero vector.
Proof 6.1 determines the constant derivative on the four coordinate directions and Proof 7.1 transports it to V. The identity map is an instance of the converse in Proof 1.2.
Proof 1.1 uses nondegeneracy and rank-nullity to prove the derivative invertible; Proof 4.1 uses its four columns as a basis to force each second partial to zero.

boundaries.reason: The Statement takes a $C^2$ map on all of $A$; no interval endpoint or boundary of the domain is involved.

boundaries.evidence: Proof 5.1 and 6.1 apply the zero-total-derivative theorem on the convex open chart R4, not an unstated integration argument; only finitely many basis vectors are used.
Steps 1.1-7.1 prove the forward direction: every $C^2$ $\eta$-preserving map is affine with a linear Lorentz part.
Step 8.1 (with step 1.2) proves the converse: every affine Lorentz map is $C^\infty$ and preserves $\eta$ via its differential.

risk_review.notes: All nine steps checked: C2 regularity and nondegenerate metric make each D Phi a basis isometry. Differentiated metric coefficients C_ijk are symmetric in the first two indices and antisymmetric in the last two, hence vanish for every repeated/distinct triple. All second derivatives then vanish by nondegeneracy and the Jacobian basis. Zero derivative on convex open R4 gives one constant derivative L and translation b globally. Conjugation E L E^{-1} acts on p-o=E(x(p)) in V. Affine converse is smooth and metric-preserving; bijectivity follows, without assuming it initially.

citations.quote: **(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map $L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that $$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$ The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with a chosen time
orientation $C^+$, and let $L:V\to V$ be a linear map with
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]). Then:

(i) $L$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$; for every ordered $\eta$-orthonormal
basis the matrix $M$ of $L$ satisfies $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ with
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and conversely every invertible matrix
$M$ with $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ is the matrix of a linear Lorentz map in that
basis.

(ii) $\det L=\pm1$. The composition of two Lorentz maps is a Lorentz map, the
identity is a Lorentz map, and the inverse of a Lorentz map is a Lorentz map;
the sets $SO(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):\det L=1\}$,
$O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):L(C^+)=C^+\}$ and
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)=SO(V,\eta)\cap O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta)$ are subgroups of
$O(V,\eta)$, which itself is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL(V)$.

(iii) $\eta(Lv,Lv)=\eta(v,v)$ for all $v\in V$; hence $L$ preserves the causal
character of every nonzero vector (timelike, null or spacelike) and maps the
set of null vectors onto itself. If $L$ is proper, then the oriented volume
form is preserved:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,\dots,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]); if
$\det L=-1$ the two sides differ by the sign $-1$.

(iv) $L(C^+)$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$ of the timelike set, so
exactly one of $L(C^+)=C^+$ and $L(C^+)=C^-$ holds; $L$ is orthochronous in
the first case and non-orthochronous in the second, and $L(C^+)=C^+$ holds if
and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

(v) The affine Lorentz maps of
[[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]] form a group under composition: the
composition and the inverse of affine Lorentz maps are affine Lorentz maps,
and every affine Lorentz map is a bijection of $A$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])

derivations.claim: L is the unique linear map with L(e_a) = e'_a, is a linear Lorentz map with matrix M, and Le_0 = e'_0.
The transition is the affine map u -> M^{-1}(u - x(o')) with linear part M^{-1}.
For proper orthochronous L and c in A, (c;Le0,...,Le3) is inertial with x_L(p)=M_L^{-1}(x(p)-x(c)), where M_L=E^{-1} L E.
det M = +1.
L(C^+) = C^+, so L is orthochronous.
M^{-1} is the matrix of the proper orthochronous Lorentz map L^{-1}.
The linear part A=M^{-1} preserves q and the future causal coordinate cone. For affine F, F(u)-F(v)=A(u-v), so q and future causality are preserved on coordinate displacements.
Clauses (i)-(iii) follow, including the converse that every proper orthochronous L and c produce exactly these transitions.

boundaries.reason: No construction here ranges over an empty family: two fixed inertial frames are given and the coordinates of an event are a 4-tuple, so no empty index set, empty sum or empty product occurs.

boundaries.evidence: Step 4.1 includes zero in the closed cone and fixes it by the linear part, excluding it from causal vectors. F(0) need not be zero: preservation is applied to F(u)-F(v)=M^{-1}(u-v).

Unit elements appear explicitly: the frame basis vectors are eta-orthonormal with eta(e_0,e_0) = -1 in step 1.1, the determinant +1 of L is the properness value in step 2.1, and the affine identity corresponds to c = o with L = identity in step 1.3.

Degenerate behaviour is controlled: det L = 0 is excluded by det L = +-1 from [L2] used in step 2.1, so M and M^{-1} are invertible and the transition is a bijection; the null boundary of the cone is included in step 4.1 by q(w) = q(u) <= 0 together with w^0 >= 0.

The cone endpoints are the null vectors: step 4.1 uses non-strict inequalities q(u) <= 0 and u^0 >= 0 together with z^0 >= |z_vec|, so null coordinate vectors are mapped to null coordinate vectors and the closed cone is preserved at its boundary.

boundaries.reason: No choice principle is used: L is defined by a formula from the two given frames, M is the given change-of-basis matrix, and the inverse and cone arguments are explicit computations.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.2 uses the forward direction of the equivalence L(C^+) = C^+ if and only if L(C^+) is contained in C^+, and step 4.1 proves q(M^{-1}u) = q(u) as an identity in both directions.
Step 4.1 applies the cone calculation also to A^{-1}=M, proving onto preservation by the linear part, hence preservation of causal displacements in either chart direction.

risk_review.notes: All eight steps checked: E′=EM and L=E′E^{-1}, so M represents L while the passive chart transition uses M^{-1}; translations act only on events and cancel for differences. Orthonormality, positive basis orientation and future e0 give properness and orthochrony. The converse correctly uses M_L=E^{-1}LE. Closed cones contain zero; future causal vectors exclude it, and invertibility preserves nonzero vectors. Cauchy-Schwarz gives the nonnegative time component, including null boundaries.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be two inertial frames with
charts $x$, $x'$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Let $M$ be the
change-of-basis matrix defined by $e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$. Then:

(i) $M$ is the matrix, in the ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$, of a linear
Lorentz map $L:V\to V$, that is $L(e_a)=e'_a$ for all $a$; $M$ is proper and
orthochronous: $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$, $\det M=+1$, and $M$ maps the future cone
onto the future cone. The same holds for $M^{-1}$, the matrix of $L^{-1}$.

(ii) The chart transition $F:=x'\circ x^{-1}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$
is the affine map $F(u)=M^{-1}(u-x(o'))$, whose linear part $M^{-1}$ is a
proper orthochronous Lorentz matrix. For any $u,v\in\mathbb R^4$ one has
$F(u)-F(v)=M^{-1}(u-v)$ and $q(F(u)-F(v))=q(u-v)$, where
$q(d):=\eta_0(d,d)=-(d^0)^2+|d_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2$. In particular, if
$u-v$ is future causal (that is $u-v\neq0$ and
$u^0-v^0\ge|u_{\mathrm{vec}}-v_{\mathrm{vec}}|$), then $F(u)-F(v)$ is
future causal. Thus causal displacements are preserved; the linear part
maps the future causal coordinate cone onto itself.

(iii) Conversely, for every proper orthochronous linear Lorentz map
$L:V\to V$ and every point $c\in A$, the tuple
$(c;Le_0,Le_1,Le_2,Le_3)$ is an inertial frame, and, writing $M_L:=E^{-1}\circ L\circ E:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$, where $E(u)=\sum_a u^ae_a$, its chart satisfies $x_L(p)=M_L^{-1}(x(p)-x(c))$ for all $p\in A$. Hence the transitions from the
chart $x$ are exactly the affine maps $u\mapsto M_L^{-1}(u-x(c))$ with $L$
ranging over the proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps and $c$ over $A$,
and the linear parts of transitions are exactly the proper orthochronous
Lorentz matrices and their inverses.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with a chosen time
orientation $C^+$, and let $L:V\to V$ be a linear map with
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]). Then:

(i) $L$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$; for every ordered $\eta$-orthonormal
basis the matrix $M$ of $L$ satisfies $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ with
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and conversely every invertible matrix
$M$ with $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ is the matrix of a linear Lorentz map in that
basis.

(ii) $\det L=\pm1$. The composition of two Lorentz maps is a Lorentz map, the
identity is a Lorentz map, and the inverse of a Lorentz map is a Lorentz map;
the sets $SO(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):\det L=1\}$,
$O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):L(C^+)=C^+\}$ and
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)=SO(V,\eta)\cap O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta)$ are subgroups of
$O(V,\eta)$, which itself is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL(V)$.

(iii) $\eta(Lv,Lv)=\eta(v,v)$ for all $v\in V$; hence $L$ preserves the causal
character of every nonzero vector (timelike, null or spacelike) and maps the
set of null vectors onto itself. If $L$ is proper, then the oriented volume
form is preserved:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,\dots,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]); if
$\det L=-1$ the two sides differ by the sign $-1$.

(iv) $L(C^+)$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$ of the timelike set, so
exactly one of $L(C^+)=C^+$ and $L(C^+)=C^-$ holds; $L$ is orthochronous in
the first case and non-orthochronous in the second, and $L(C^+)=C^+$ holds if
and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

(v) The affine Lorentz maps of
[[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]] form a group under composition: the
composition and the inverse of affine Lorentz maps are affine Lorentz maps,
and every affine Lorentz map is a bijection of $A$.

Let $S=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be the spatial three-space of a frame
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with its Euclidean structure $\delta$
([[def-spatial-rotation-of-an-inertial-frame]]), and let $e\in S$ be a unit
vector, $\delta(e,e)=1$. Define $J:\mathbb R^3\to S$ by
$J(a):=\sum_{i=1}^3a_i e_i$, where $a_i:=a(i-1)$ relabels the coordinates
$0,1,2$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Let $n:=J^{-1}(e)$; then
$|n|=1$, since $\delta(J(a),J(b))=a\cdot b$ by orthonormality.
For $t\in(-1,1)$, the notation $B(te)$ means $B(tn)$, whose parameter
belongs to $\mathbb R^3$, while $e$ belongs to $V$.
Let $\beta_1,\beta_2\in(-1,1)$ be real parameters and
let $B(\beta_1e)$ and $B(\beta_2e)$ be the corresponding passive boosts
([[def-lorentz-boost]]). Then

$$B(\beta_1e)\,B(\beta_2e)=B(\beta e),\qquad \beta:=\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2},$$

and $|\beta|<1$. In particular the two collinear boosts commute,
$B(\beta_1e)B(\beta_2e)=B(\beta_2e)B(\beta_1e)$, and

$$B(\beta_1e)\,B(-\beta_2e)=B\!\left(\frac{\beta_1-\beta_2}{1-\beta_1\beta_2}\,e\right).$$

The composed parameter $\beta$ is the displayed rational expression, which
generally differs from $\beta_1+\beta_2$; this algebraic law is conventionally
called velocity addition. In particular,
no composition of two boosts in a common direction leaves the open interval
$(-1,1)$: the composed parameter always satisfies $|\beta|<1$.

3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

This framework fixes the following SI coordinate and unit conventions for the
oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ and its inertial
charts ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]],
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

1. **Adopted conversion constant.** The framework uses a positive constant $c$
   with unit metre per second, $\mathrm m/\mathrm s$, interpreted as the
   **speed of light in vacuum** under the framework's light postulate. In SI
   its numerical value is exactly $299\,792\,458$ by the definition of the
   metre (BIPM, *SI defining constants*, table row $c$). This exact unit
   convention does not prove that the ideal-light model describes nature;
   measurements and realizations of units still have uncertainty.
2. **Coordinates.** In every inertial chart $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ define the
   coordinate-time map $t:A\to\mathbb R$ by $t(p)=x^0(p)/c$, with unit second
   $\mathrm s$, and assign unit metre $\mathrm m$ to every $x^a$. An **at-rest
   line of this frame** is $s\mapsto o+cs e_0+\sum_{i=1}^3r^ie_i$, $s\in\mathbb R$,
   for fixed spatial coordinates $(r^1,r^2,r^3)$ in metres; its coordinate
   time is $s$. Interpreting coordinate-time differences as readings of
   synchronized ideal clocks on these lines is a physical assumption stated
   in the clock postulate, not a consequence of assigning units.
3. **Metric components.** The matrix $\eta_{ab}=\eta(e_a,e_b)$ in the frame is
   $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ with **dimensionless** entries. Thus
   $I(p,q)=\eta(q-p,q-p)=-(\Delta x^0)^2+\sum_{i=1}^3(\Delta x^i)^2$
   carries unit $\mathrm m^2$.
4. **Proper time of a straight segment.** For a timelike displacement $q-p$,
   the affine straight segment is $s\mapsto p+s(q-p)$, $s\in[0,1]$. Define its
   positive **proper-time length** as

   $$\tau:=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}.$$

   It has unit second, since $c^{-1}$ converts the square-root interval in
   metres into seconds. This length is positive even if the segment is
   oriented toward the past; a physical advancing clock uses future orientation.
5. **Kinematic bookkeeping.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval
   with parameter $\tau$ in seconds, and let $\gamma:J\to A$ have $C^2$
   coordinates $y=x\circ\gamma:J\to\mathbb R^4$
   ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). With
   $E(u)=\sum_au^ae_a$, require $U(\tau):=E(y'(\tau))\in C^+$ and
   $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$. This is the **proper-time normalization** used here for
   units; the general construction of a proper-time parameter is developed
   later. The **four-velocity** is $U:J\to V$, with components $U^a=(y^a)'$
   and unit $\mathrm m/\mathrm s$. The **four-acceleration** is
   $\mathcal A=E(y''):J\to V$, with unit $\mathrm m/\mathrm s^2$.
   For a positive constant mass parameter $m$ in kilograms, define
   **four-momentum** $P=mU:J\to V$, with unit
   $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m/\mathrm s$, and **energy measured by this frame**
   $\mathcal E=cP^0=-c\eta(e_0,P):J\to\mathbb R$, with unit joule
   $\mathrm J=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^2/\mathrm s^2$. The equality follows from
   $\eta(e_0,P)=-P^0$. These are definitions for dimensional bookkeeping;
   the physical particle interpretation and dynamics belong to later pages.
6. **Temporal-coordinate convention.** Replacing $x^0$ by $t=x^0/c$ pulls
   the interval expression back to $-c^2(\Delta t)^2+\sum_i(\Delta x^i)^2$.
   Thus $g_{tt}=-c^2$ has unit $\mathrm m^2/\mathrm s^2$, the spatial
   components remain dimensionless, and mixed time-space components have unit
   $\mathrm m/\mathrm s$ (and equal zero in this inertial chart). Formulas
   must be transformed when changing this convention.
7. **Natural units.** A presentation with $c=1$ identifies temporal and spatial
   units by this conversion factor; it requires an explicit restoration table
   for $c$. It does not assert that the SI numerical value of $c$ is $1$.

**Status.** These are conventions and dimensional bookkeeping for the model.
The SI numerical value of $c$ is exact by unit definition; the physical
interpretation and applicability of the model remain adopted and empirically
testable. SI unit status does not make a quantity primitive in the theory.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with its inertial chart
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Every $v\in V$ has a unique
coordinate vector $(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ with $v=\sum_av^ae_a$. For an ordered
$4$-tuple $(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ of vectors of $V$ let

$$[v_j^a]:=\begin{pmatrix}v_0^0&v_1^0&v_2^0&v_3^0\\ v_0^1&v_1^1&v_2^1&v_3^1\\ v_0^2&v_1^2&v_2^2&v_3^2\\ v_0^3&v_1^3&v_2^3&v_3^3\end{pmatrix}$$

be the $4\times4$ real matrix whose $j$-th column lists the coordinates of
$v_j$ in the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, and define

$$\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3):=\det\bigl([v_j^a]\bigr)$$

by the determinant of a square matrix
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]). Then $\epsilon$ is an **alternating
$4$-linear form** on $V$
([[def-alternating-k-linear-map]]): the determinant is multilinear and
alternating in the columns, so replacing one $v_j$ by $\lambda v_j+\mu w$
replaces the $j$-th column correspondingly and $\epsilon$ is linear in each
argument, and $\epsilon(v_0,\ldots,v_3)=0$ whenever two arguments coincide,
since then two columns coincide
([[thm-determinant-is-the-unique-normalized-alternating-multilinear-function]]).
The form $\epsilon$ is the **oriented volume form of the model**. Its
well-definedness as a form of the model, independent of the inertial frame used
in the display, is proved in [[lem-volume-form-is-independent-of-the-oriented-frame]].

**Components.** Write $\epsilon_{abcd}:=\epsilon(e_a,e_b,e_c,e_d)$ for the
components of $\epsilon$ in the inertial frame. Evaluating the determinant on
the coordinate matrix of $(e_a,e_b,e_c,e_d)$, which is the permutation matrix
of the tuple, gives

$$\epsilon_{0123}=+1,\qquad \epsilon_{abcd}=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\ \text{ if }(a,b,c,d)=(\sigma(0),\sigma(1),\sigma(2),\sigma(3))\ \text{ for a permutation }\sigma,$$

and $\epsilon_{abcd}=0$ whenever two of the indices coincide; these are the
**permutation symbols** of the frame. Indeed the coordinate vector of $e_a$ is
the $a$-th standard basis vector, so the coordinate matrix of
$(e_a,e_b,e_c,e_d)$ is the permutation matrix of the tuple and its determinant
is $+1$ on the identity tuple, the sign of the permutation otherwise, and $0$
when two indices repeat.

**Raised components.** The **inverse metric** $\eta^{ab}$ is the inverse of the
matrix $\eta_{ab}:=\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$, which
exists because $\eta$ is nondegenerate
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]); it is again
$\eta^{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)^{ab}$. The raised components of the
volume form are

$$\epsilon^{abcd}:=\eta^{aa'}\eta^{bb'}\eta^{cc'}\eta^{dd'}\epsilon_{a'b'c'd'}$$

(summation over repeated primed indices). Since the inverse metric is diagonal
with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$, only one term contributes to $\epsilon^{0123}$
and

$$\epsilon^{0123}=\eta^{00}\eta^{11}\eta^{22}\eta^{33}\epsilon_{0123}=(-1)(+1)(+1)(+1)(+1)=-1 .$$

**Spatial symbol.** The **spatial permutation symbol** $\epsilon_{ijk}$ for
$i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$ is defined by $\epsilon_{123}=+1$ together with alternation
in the three indices; explicitly $\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ for even permutations of
$(1,2,3)$, $\epsilon_{ijk}=-1$ for odd permutations, and $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$
whenever two of $i,j,k$ coincide.

An **inertial change of description** is such a map
$F$ whose linear part $L$ satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\quad\text{for all }v,w\in V,\qquad \det L=+1\ \text{relative to the fixed orientation of }V,\qquad L(C^+)=C^+ .$$

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements, with the SI coordinate and unit conventions of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(i) Ideal clocks.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate interval and
$\gamma:I\to A$ a curve. Choose an inertial chart $\chi$ with
$E(u)=\sum_au^ae_a$ as in [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Require
$y:=\chi\circ\gamma:I\to\mathbb R^4$ to be $C^1$ on the interior of $I$,
with its derivative extending continuously to any included endpoints, where
it is the one-sided derivative. Define the displacement-valued derivative by
$\dot\gamma(s):=E(y'(s))\in V$ and require $\dot\gamma(s)\in C^+$ everywhere,
including such endpoints. This derivative is chart-independent: a second
chart has coordinates $\widetilde y=M^{-1}(y-\chi(o'))$, so its
parameter derivative is $M^{-1}\mathrm dy/\mathrm ds$, while its basis map
is $E'=EM$; their product is $E\,\mathrm dy/\mathrm ds$.

An **ideal clock on this curve** has a reading map $\sigma:I\to\mathbb R$
in seconds, specified up to an additive constant, with, for all $a<b$ in $I$,

$$\sigma(b)-\sigma(a)=c^{-1}\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta\bigl(\dot\gamma(s),\dot\gamma(s)\bigr)}\,\mathrm ds .$$

The integrand is positive and continuous on $[a,b]$: the coordinate derivatives
are continuous, $\eta$ is a finite bilinear expression, and the square root
is continuous at every positive argument, as follows from
$|\sqrt r-\sqrt q|=|r-q|/(\sqrt r+\sqrt q)$ for $r,q>0$.
Thus [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]] applies to this compact interval
and gives a well-defined Riemann integral. The reading rule contains no
additional acceleration-dependent correction (**clock hypothesis**); it does
not require $C^2$ regularity or an acceleration to exist. This is an adopted
physical interpretation of the length integral, not a proof about real clocks.

**(ii) Ideal light.** In vacuum, the **ideal light rays** are the oriented
straight lines parametrized by $\ell:\mathbb R\to A$,
$\ell(\lambda)=p+\lambda v$, where $p\in A$ and $v\in V$ is future null;
increasing $\lambda$ specifies their future direction. In an inertial chart
$\chi$ their coordinate map is

$$\chi(\ell(\lambda))=\chi(p)+\lambda\,(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3).$$

Since the chart's time-axis vector is future, the cone description of
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] gives
$v^0=\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert>0$. With $t=\chi^0/c$ the spatial
coordinate velocity is $c(v^1,v^2,v^3)/v^0$ and has Euclidean magnitude $c$
in every inertial chart. The conversion constant is the same across charts;
its exact SI numerical value is a unit convention as specified in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], while the ideal-vacuum-light
interpretation is an adopted, empirically testable model assumption.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

derivations.claim: By [L1], the transition is $x'(p)=M^{-1}(x(p)-x(o'))$, the affine map $u\mapsto M^{-1}u-M^{-1}x(o')$ with linear part $\Lambda:=M^{-1}$, the matrix of the linear Lorentz map $L^{-1}$, which is proper orthochronous by [L1] and [L2]. For events $p,q$ the affine formula gives $\Delta'=x'(q)-x'(p)=M^{-1}(x(q)-x(p))=\Lambda\Delta$. Since the matrix $\Lambda$ of the Lorentz map $L^{-1}$ satisfies $\eta_0(\Lambda a,\Lambda b)=\eta_0(a,b)$ for all coordinate columns $a,b$ (the matrix form of the defining Lorentz property), $\eta_0(\Delta',\Delta')=\eta_0(\Lambda\Delta,\Lambda\Delta)=\eta_0(\Delta,\Delta)$, which is exactly $I(p,q)$ by [L4] and [L5]. Hence the interval computed from coordinates does not depend on the inertial chart, proving (i).

For (iv), the volume form is preserved because its argument transforms by the proper linear Lorentz map with matrix $\Lambda$: put $\widetilde L:=E\circ\Lambda\circ E^{-1}:V\to V$. Writing $v_j=E a_j$ with coordinate columns $a_j$, the definition [L7] and the volume-form clause of [L2] give $\epsilon(E\Lambda a_0,\dots,E\Lambda a_3)=\epsilon(\widetilde Lv_0,\dots,\widetilde Lv_3)=\det(\widetilde L)\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$, since $\det\Lambda=+1$; the same computation shows that the orientation (the sign of the transition determinant) is preserved. The composition of two inertial transitions is again an inertial transition: if $x,x',x''$ are inertial charts, both $x''\circ x'^{-1}$ and $x'\circ x^{-1}$ are bijections, so their composite is $x''\circ x^{-1}$, the transition from $x$ to $x''$, which by [L1] is affine with proper orthochronous linear part. Finally, if the two transitions have linear parts $B(\beta_1e)$ and $B(\beta_2e)$ with parameters in a common spatial direction $e$, then the composite has linear part $B(\beta_1e)B(\beta_2e)=B\bigl(\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2}e\bigr)$ by [L3], and the reverse order gives the same result because collinear boosts commute. This proves (iv).

The classification of $\Delta$ is read from the sign of $\eta_0(\Delta,\Delta)$: it is timelike when this number is negative, null when it is zero and $\Delta\neq0$, spacelike when it is positive, by [L6] and the coordinate expression $\eta(v,w)=v^{T}\eta_0w$ in an inertial frame; the zero displacement $\Delta=0$ is none of the three and remains $0$ under every linear transition, so the classification statement is trivially chart-independent in that case. By step 1.1 the number $\eta_0(\Delta,\Delta)$ is unchanged under the transition, so the classification, and with it the sign of the interval, is chart-independent. For the future/past distinction, for a nonzero causal displacement, $q-p$ corresponds to a nonzero column $\Delta$, which is future causal exactly when $E\Delta\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)\setminus\{0\}$; applying the linear map with matrix $\Lambda$ to a future causal coordinate vector gives a future causal coordinate vector by [L1], and applying the same statement to the inverse transition (whose linear part is $\Lambda^{-1}$) gives the converse, so future-relatedness is chart-independent. For the past case, $x\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ holds exactly when $-x\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$, by the coordinate descriptions $v^0\le-|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ and $(-v)^0\ge|(-v)_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ from the cone lemma in [L2]; since $\Lambda(-\Delta)=-\Lambda\Delta$, the argument of the previous sentence applied to $-\Delta$ shows that past-relatedness is chart-independent as well. This proves (ii).

Let $\gamma(\lambda)=p+\lambda v$ be an ideal vacuum light ray with $v$ future null, so that in the chart $x$ its coordinate image is $x(p)+\lambda v_x$ with $v_x$ the coordinate column of $v$, a straight line of future null coordinate direction by [L9] and step 2.1. Under the transition the image is $x'(p)+\lambda\Lambda v_x$ by step 1.1: again a straight line, with direction $w:=\Lambda v_x$. The vector with coordinates $w$ is the image under the Lorentz map $L^{-1}$ of the future null vector $v$, hence is future null by [L2] for nullness and by the future-causal preservation of [L1]; therefore the coordinate image is again a future null straight line, and applying the same argument to the inverse transition shows that the class of such lines is preserved in both directions. The coordinate speed statement is then the content of the light clause [L9] applied in the chart $x'$: for the future null direction $w$ one has $w^0=|w_{\mathrm{vec}}|>0$, so $|\Delta x_{\mathrm{vec}}|/\Delta t=c$ for $\lambda_2>\lambda_1$, since $\Delta t=(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)w^0/c>0$ and $|\Delta x_{\mathrm{vec}}|=(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)|w_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ in every inertial chart. This proves (iii).

Clauses (i)-(iv) are steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1 and 1.2. Every step is a conditional deduction from the adopted postulates [L8], [L9] and the mathematical suppliers; no step asserts an empirical measurement, and the idealizations listed in the Statement's qualification are carried by [L9].

boundaries.reason: The statement quantifies over events and inertial charts of the model; it asserts nothing about an empty class of objects.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 treats the zero displacement $\Delta=0$, which has invariant interval $0$ and is classified in none of the three causal classes.
Step 3.1 records the light-line normalization: the coordinate speed equals $c$ in every inertial chart for the single class of future null straight lines.
Step 2.1 separates the spacelike case, where no future relation is defined, from the causal cases, so the degenerate exclusive alternative is handled.

boundaries.reason: All claims are pointwise statements about events and charts, with no interval endpoint or limiting parameter.
The proof fixes two inertial charts and uses the explicit affine transition; no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 proves the forward chart-independence of the interval and step 2.1 the forward chart-independence of the causal classification and the future/past relation.
Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 apply the same transition to the inverse chart pair, giving the converse directions.

risk_review.notes: All five steps checked under adopted covariance and ideal-light/clock assumptions: coordinate translations cancel on differences, Lambda=M^{-1} preserves eta0, inverse transitions give both directions of causal/time-orientation invariance, and zero displacement stays outside timelike/null/spacelike classes. Positive null parameter increments give Delta t>0 and speed c. E Lambda E^{-1} transports the oriented volume form correctly. Composition law is restricted to pure common-axis boost linear parts. No empirical input or statistical certainty is asserted; the SI number is a convention.
risk_review.sources_checked: Current carrier, exact cited dependency definitions/statements, reader-2 and refute-2 evidence; source sections recorded in adjudication report.

boundaries.evidence: The Definition now permits empty open Omega and specifies its unique empty field of each type. For nonempty Omega the zero constant component array gives a field.
The Definition includes $r=s=0$ (scalar fields) and the regularity cases $k=0$ (continuous) and the zero tensor field; the empty index list is admitted by the type-$(r,s)$ convention.
The Definition names the cases $r=1,s=0$ (vector fields) and $r=0,s=1$ (covector fields) explicitly, with the single-index component laws.
The Definition handles the degenerate cases through the identification $T_pA=V$ and the component formula; a tensor with repeated indices is a component label, not a separate object.
The Definition admits both endpoint values of the regularity parameter: $k=0$ (continuous) and $k=\infty$ (smooth), and no limiting operation is involved.

boundaries.reason: The Definition introduces a map and its components; it selects no element from any family, so no choice is used.

boundaries.evidence: The Definition states that $T$ is $\mathcal C^k$ if and only if all components in one, equivalently every, inertial chart are $\mathcal C^k$; the forward direction uses the linearity of the frame comparisons.
The reverse direction of the Definition's equivalence uses the affine smooth chart transitions to convert component regularity into regularity of the field.

risk_review.notes: The entire Definition checked: multilinear expansion is a two-sided inverse of the finite component map, giving dimension N=4^(r+s)≥1 even for scalar rank. The empty domain has its unique empty field. Finite norm equivalence and completeness suppliers apply at positive N; iterated partial/total derivative equivalence follows by induction on finite coordinate arrays. Constant basis changes and affine precomposition preserve every Ck order in both directions, including k=0 and infinity. The manifold domain is converted explicitly through x^{-1}, not treated as a Banach space.
