Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be two inertial frames with
charts $x$, $x'$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Let $M$ be the
change-of-basis matrix defined by $e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$. Then:

(i) $M$ is the matrix, in the ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$, of a linear
Lorentz map $L:V\to V$, that is $L(e_a)=e'_a$ for all $a$; $M$ is proper and
orthochronous: $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$, $\det M=+1$, and $M$ maps the future cone
onto the future cone. The same holds for $M^{-1}$, the matrix of $L^{-1}$.

(ii) The chart transition $F:=x'\circ x^{-1}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$
is the affine map $F(u)=M^{-1}(u-x(o'))$, whose linear part $M^{-1}$ is a
proper orthochronous Lorentz matrix. For any $u,v\in\mathbb R^4$ one has
$F(u)-F(v)=M^{-1}(u-v)$ and $q(F(u)-F(v))=q(u-v)$, where
$q(d):=\eta_0(d,d)=-(d^0)^2+|d_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2$. In particular, if
$u-v$ is future causal (that is $u-v\neq0$ and
$u^0-v^0\ge|u_{\mathrm{vec}}-v_{\mathrm{vec}}|$), then $F(u)-F(v)$ is
future causal. Thus causal displacements are preserved; the linear part
maps the future causal coordinate cone onto itself.

(iii) Conversely, for every proper orthochronous linear Lorentz map
$L:V\to V$ and every point $c\in A$, the tuple
$(c;Le_0,Le_1,Le_2,Le_3)$ is an inertial frame, and, writing $M_L:=E^{-1}\circ L\circ E:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$, where $E(u)=\sum_a u^ae_a$, its chart satisfies $x_L(p)=M_L^{-1}(x(p)-x(c))$ for all $p\in A$. Hence the transitions from the
chart $x$ are exactly the affine maps $u\mapsto M_L^{-1}(u-x(c))$ with $L$
ranging over the proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps and $c$ over $A$,
and the linear parts of transitions are exactly the proper orthochronous
Lorentz matrices and their inverses.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with a chosen time
orientation $C^+$, and let $L:V\to V$ be a linear map with
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]). Then:

(i) $L$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$; for every ordered $\eta$-orthonormal
basis the matrix $M$ of $L$ satisfies $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ with
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and conversely every invertible matrix
$M$ with $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ is the matrix of a linear Lorentz map in that
basis.

(ii) $\det L=\pm1$. The composition of two Lorentz maps is a Lorentz map, the
identity is a Lorentz map, and the inverse of a Lorentz map is a Lorentz map;
the sets $SO(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):\det L=1\}$,
$O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):L(C^+)=C^+\}$ and
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)=SO(V,\eta)\cap O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta)$ are subgroups of
$O(V,\eta)$, which itself is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL(V)$.

(iii) $\eta(Lv,Lv)=\eta(v,v)$ for all $v\in V$; hence $L$ preserves the causal
character of every nonzero vector (timelike, null or spacelike) and maps the
set of null vectors onto itself. If $L$ is proper, then the oriented volume
form is preserved:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,\dots,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]); if
$\det L=-1$ the two sides differ by the sign $-1$.

(iv) $L(C^+)$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$ of the timelike set, so
exactly one of $L(C^+)=C^+$ and $L(C^+)=C^-$ holds; $L$ is orthochronous in
the first case and non-orthochronous in the second, and $L(C^+)=C^+$ holds if
and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

(v) The affine Lorentz maps of
[[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]] form a group under composition: the
composition and the inverse of affine Lorentz maps are affine Lorentz maps,
and every affine Lorentz map is a bijection of $A$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space of
[[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], with its inertial smooth structure
([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]], [[def-smooth-manifold]]).
Let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be open, let $r,s\in\mathbb N$, and let
$k\in\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$. Empty $\Omega$ is allowed; it has the unique
empty field of each type.

Write $T^{r,s}(V)$ for the real vector space, under pointwise operations, of
multilinear maps $(V^*)^r\times V^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]],
[[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]). Identify $T_pA$ with $V$ by
[[lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v]]. For an inertial frame
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with chart $x$, let $(e^{*a})$ be its dual basis,
defined by $e^{*a}(e_b)=\delta^a_b$
([[def-dual-family-associated-to-a-basis]]). The components of a map
$T:\Omega\to T^{r,s}(V)$ are

$$T^{a_1\dots a_r}{}_{b_1\dots b_s}(p):=T(p)(e^{*a_1},\dots,e^{*a_r},e_{b_1},\dots,e_{b_s}).$$

A **$\mathcal C^k$ type-$(r,s)$ tensor field on $\Omega$** is such a map for
which each component, regarded as a function of $u=x(p)$ on the open set
$x(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, is of class $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; for $k=\infty$ all finite
orders are required.

**Finite-dimensional construction and intrinsic regularity.** Put
$N=4^{r+s}\ge1$, with the component array ordered lexicographically. Every
array of $N$ real numbers defines exactly one tensor: expand each input as
$\alpha_i=\sum_a\alpha_i(e_a)e^{*a}$ and
$v_j=\sum_b e^{*b}(v_j)e_b$, then sum the array entries multiplied by
$\prod_i\alpha_i(e_{a_i})\prod_j e^{*b_j}(v_j)$. This is multilinear and
recovers the array by evaluation on the indicated basis inputs; multilinearity
forces the same formula for any tensor. Thus the component map is a linear
isomorphism $T^{r,s}(V)\to\mathbb R^N$. Pulling back the Euclidean norm gives
a norm on this space ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), and every norm makes it
Banach by [[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]]. Any two norms
are equivalent by transporting them to $\mathbb R^N$ and applying
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]].

A change of inertial frame expresses each new basis and dual-basis vector as
a constant finite linear combination of the old ones; multilinearity therefore
makes the new component array an invertible constant linear transformation of
the old array. The coordinate precomposition is an invertible affine map by
[[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]. Finite linear combinations
and affine precomposition preserve $C^k$: each first derivative follows from
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], and successive derivatives repeat
that rule with constant affine coefficients. Applying the inverse transformations
proves the converse. Hence the definition is independent of frame. Continuous
partials give total derivatives by
[[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], and
induction on order gives the equivalent finite-dimensional Banach-space
$C^k$ definition of [[def-c-k-map-between-banach-spaces]] for $T\circ x^{-1}$.
The norm equivalence inequalities preserve the derivative remainder limits and
continuity of each iterated derivative, so this formulation is also independent
of norm. No definition of a Banach-space map with manifold domain is presumed.

A type-$(0,0)$ field is a **scalar field**, a $C^k$ real-valued function.
A type-$(1,0)$ field is a **vector field**, with the vector $v$ identified with
$\alpha\mapsto\alpha(v)$: conversely a linear functional $Q$ on $V^*$ has
$v=\sum_aQ(e^{*a})e_a$ and $Q(\alpha)=\alpha(v)$. A type-$(0,1)$ field is a
**covector field**, taking values in $V^*$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space, and let $r,s\ge 0$. A
**type $(r,s)$ tensor on $V$** is a multilinear map

$$T:(V^*)^r\times V^s\to\mathbb R.$$

With this convention, vectors are type $(1,0)$ tensors and covectors are type
$(0,1)$ tensors.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space, and let $r,s\ge 0$. A
**type $(r,s)$ tensor on $V$** is a multilinear map

$$T:(V^*)^r\times V^s\to\mathbb R.$$

With this convention, vectors are type $(1,0)$ tensors and covectors are type
$(0,1)$ tensors.

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. A **linear functional** on $V$ is a linear map $f:V\to F$, where $F$ is regarded as a vector space over itself. The **algebraic dual space** of $V$ is

$$V^*:=\mathcal L(V,F),$$

with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. This is the full algebraic dual: no topology, norm, or continuity condition is imposed.

Let $T$ be a type $(r,s)$ tensor on $V$ with $r,s\ge 1$. Contracting the first
contravariant slot against the first covariant slot gives the type
$(r-1,s-1)$ tensor $\operatorname{ctr}(T)$ defined intrinsically by

$$ \operatorname{ctr}(T)(\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_r,v_2,\ldots,v_s) :=\sum_i T(e^i,\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_r,e_i,v_2,\ldots,v_s), $$

where $(e_i)$ is any basis of $V$ and $(e^i)$ its dual basis. The next lemma
shows that this formula is basis-independent.

The contraction formula

$$ \sum_i T(e^i,\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_r,e_i,v_2,\ldots,v_s) $$

has the same value for every basis $(e_i)$ and its dual basis $(e^i)$.

Let $F$ be a field and let $V,W$ be $F$-vector spaces ([[def-vector-space]]). For $k\ge0$, a map

$$f:V^k\longrightarrow W$$

is **$k$-linear** (multilinear) when it is linear in each of its $k$ arguments separately, with the other arguments held fixed. It is **alternating** when

$$f(v_1,\ldots,v_k)=0\qquad\text{whenever }v_i=v_j\text{ for some }1\le i<j\le k.$$

For $k=0$, a $0$-linear map is a choice of one element of $W$; for $k=1$, a $1$-linear map is a linear map. Both are alternating vacuously, because there is no pair of arguments to compare.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with its inertial chart
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Every $v\in V$ has a unique
coordinate vector $(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ with $v=\sum_av^ae_a$. For an ordered
$4$-tuple $(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ of vectors of $V$ let

$$[v_j^a]:=\begin{pmatrix}v_0^0&v_1^0&v_2^0&v_3^0\\ v_0^1&v_1^1&v_2^1&v_3^1\\ v_0^2&v_1^2&v_2^2&v_3^2\\ v_0^3&v_1^3&v_2^3&v_3^3\end{pmatrix}$$

be the $4\times4$ real matrix whose $j$-th column lists the coordinates of
$v_j$ in the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, and define

$$\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3):=\det\bigl([v_j^a]\bigr)$$

by the determinant of a square matrix
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]). Then $\epsilon$ is an **alternating
$4$-linear form** on $V$
([[def-alternating-k-linear-map]]): the determinant is multilinear and
alternating in the columns, so replacing one $v_j$ by $\lambda v_j+\mu w$
replaces the $j$-th column correspondingly and $\epsilon$ is linear in each
argument, and $\epsilon(v_0,\ldots,v_3)=0$ whenever two arguments coincide,
since then two columns coincide
([[thm-determinant-is-the-unique-normalized-alternating-multilinear-function]]).
The form $\epsilon$ is the **oriented volume form of the model**. Its
well-definedness as a form of the model, independent of the inertial frame used
in the display, is proved in [[lem-volume-form-is-independent-of-the-oriented-frame]].

**Components.** Write $\epsilon_{abcd}:=\epsilon(e_a,e_b,e_c,e_d)$ for the
components of $\epsilon$ in the inertial frame. Evaluating the determinant on
the coordinate matrix of $(e_a,e_b,e_c,e_d)$, which is the permutation matrix
of the tuple, gives

$$\epsilon_{0123}=+1,\qquad \epsilon_{abcd}=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\ \text{ if }(a,b,c,d)=(\sigma(0),\sigma(1),\sigma(2),\sigma(3))\ \text{ for a permutation }\sigma,$$

and $\epsilon_{abcd}=0$ whenever two of the indices coincide; these are the
**permutation symbols** of the frame. Indeed the coordinate vector of $e_a$ is
the $a$-th standard basis vector, so the coordinate matrix of
$(e_a,e_b,e_c,e_d)$ is the permutation matrix of the tuple and its determinant
is $+1$ on the identity tuple, the sign of the permutation otherwise, and $0$
when two indices repeat.

**Raised components.** The **inverse metric** $\eta^{ab}$ is the inverse of the
matrix $\eta_{ab}:=\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$, which
exists because $\eta$ is nondegenerate
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]); it is again
$\eta^{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)^{ab}$. The raised components of the
volume form are

$$\epsilon^{abcd}:=\eta^{aa'}\eta^{bb'}\eta^{cc'}\eta^{dd'}\epsilon_{a'b'c'd'}$$

(summation over repeated primed indices). Since the inverse metric is diagonal
with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$, only one term contributes to $\epsilon^{0123}$
and

$$\epsilon^{0123}=\eta^{00}\eta^{11}\eta^{22}\eta^{33}\epsilon_{0123}=(-1)(+1)(+1)(+1)(+1)=-1 .$$

**Spatial symbol.** The **spatial permutation symbol** $\epsilon_{ijk}$ for
$i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$ is defined by $\epsilon_{123}=+1$ together with alternation
in the three indices; explicitly $\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ for even permutations of
$(1,2,3)$, $\epsilon_{ijk}=-1$ for odd permutations, and $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$
whenever two of $i,j,k$ coincide.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with a chosen time
orientation $C^+$, and let $L:V\to V$ be a linear map with
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]). Then:

(i) $L$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$; for every ordered $\eta$-orthonormal
basis the matrix $M$ of $L$ satisfies $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ with
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and conversely every invertible matrix
$M$ with $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ is the matrix of a linear Lorentz map in that
basis.

(ii) $\det L=\pm1$. The composition of two Lorentz maps is a Lorentz map, the
identity is a Lorentz map, and the inverse of a Lorentz map is a Lorentz map;
the sets $SO(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):\det L=1\}$,
$O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):L(C^+)=C^+\}$ and
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)=SO(V,\eta)\cap O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta)$ are subgroups of
$O(V,\eta)$, which itself is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL(V)$.

(iii) $\eta(Lv,Lv)=\eta(v,v)$ for all $v\in V$; hence $L$ preserves the causal
character of every nonzero vector (timelike, null or spacelike) and maps the
set of null vectors onto itself. If $L$ is proper, then the oriented volume
form is preserved:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,\dots,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]); if
$\det L=-1$ the two sides differ by the sign $-1$.

(iv) $L(C^+)$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$ of the timelike set, so
exactly one of $L(C^+)=C^+$ and $L(C^+)=C^-$ holds; $L$ is orthochronous in
the first case and non-orthochronous in the second, and $L(C^+)=C^+$ holds if
and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

(v) The affine Lorentz maps of
[[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]] form a group under composition: the
composition and the inverse of affine Lorentz maps are affine Lorentz maps,
and every affine Lorentz map is a bijection of $A$.

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be its coordinates, so that a vector is written
$x=x^0e_0+x^1e_1+x^2e_2+x^3e_3$ and the spatial part is the coordinate
column $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ with its standard
Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

For $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$, where
$|\boldsymbol\beta|$ is the Euclidean norm, set

$$\gamma(\boldsymbol\beta):=(1-|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)^{-1/2}\ \ge 1,$$

with equality exactly for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ and strict inequality
for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$; here the power is the rational power
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). The **passive Lorentz
boost with parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$** is the linear map
$B(\boldsymbol\beta):V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) defined by its action on
coordinates: for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$,

$$x'^0=\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}),\qquad x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\,(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})\,\boldsymbol\beta-\gamma\,\boldsymbol\beta\,x^0,$$

and for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$, $B(\mathbf 0):=\operatorname{id}_V$.
Here $x'$ denotes the coordinates of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ applied to the
vector with coordinates $x$, and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is
the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the matrix of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}\gamma & -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta & I_3+\dfrac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\,\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix},$$

that is, $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ for
$i=1,2,3$, and
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$
for $i,j=1,2,3$, with the spatial block replaced by
$I_3$ when $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$. In the $1+1$ case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\beta e_1$ this reads
$x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$ and $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$. The vector
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is called the **boost parameter**; it is dimensionless and
mathematically independent of any unit convention.

**Consistency of the definition.** The displayed formulas assign to every
coordinate pair $(x^0,x_{\mathrm{vec}})$ a pair
$(x'^0,x'_{\mathrm{vec}})$; writing the result as the matrix product above and
using that $\mathbb R^4$ is identified with coordinates through
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] (see
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), the map
$v\mapsto E(M(E^{-1}(v)))$ is the unique linear map with that matrix. The case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ is declared separately because the expression
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ is undefined there. That the two cases fit
together is the limit computation recorded next.

**The limit as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$.** For
$\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$ the identity
$\gamma^2-1=|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\gamma^2$ gives

$$\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\gamma+1}.$$

Since $|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\le3/4$ forces $1\le\gamma\le2$, the bounds
$|\beta_i|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|$ and $|\beta_i\beta_j|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$
(from the Euclidean norm convention, [[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]])
show that $\gamma\to1$ as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$; here continuity of
the positive-base power at fixed exponent $-1/2$ is
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], with real and rational powers
identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. Hence
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\to1/2$, so
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac12\beta_i\beta_j+o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)\to I$ entrywise, without a hidden division by zero.
Here $o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ denotes a remainder whose ratio to
$|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ tends to $0$ through nonzero parameters: the ratio
of each spatial remainder is bounded by
$|\gamma^2/(\gamma+1)-1/2|\to0$. The time-space entries obey
$|\gamma\beta_i|\le2|\boldsymbol\beta|\to0$, and the time-time entry tends to
$1$ by $\gamma\to1$. The
definition asserts no Lorentz property: that $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ is proved in
[[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], and its collinear
composition law in
[[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]. The physical
reading of $c\boldsymbol\beta$ as a relative velocity is not part of this
definition ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

Let $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ be the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] in an
inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. For every
$\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the following
hold.

(i) $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map:
$\eta(B(\boldsymbol\beta)v,B(\boldsymbol\beta)w)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$,
$\det B(\boldsymbol\beta)=+1$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)(C^+)=C^+$.

(ii) $B(\mathbf 0)$ is the identity, and for every $\boldsymbol\beta$ the image
of the frame vector $e_0$ is
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)e_0=\gamma\,(e_0-\beta_1e_1-\beta_2e_2-\beta_3e_3)$, so
the map $\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is injective and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ fixes $0_V$; moreover every vector $y$ with
coordinates $(0,y_{\mathrm{vec}})$ and
$\boldsymbol\beta\cdot y_{\mathrm{vec}}=0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)y=y$.

(iii) $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)B(\boldsymbol\beta)
=B(\boldsymbol\beta)B(-\boldsymbol\beta)=\operatorname{id}_V$; in particular
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is invertible with
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and
$B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ are inverse bijections of $V$.

(iv) If $u$ is a future timelike unit vector with coordinates
$(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$, so that $\eta(u,u)=-1$, $u^0>0$ and
$|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|<u^0$, then the boost with parameter
$\boldsymbol\beta:=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)u=e_0$.

(v) If a vector $x$ has $x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$, then the first coordinate of
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)x$ is $\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})>0$;
if $x^0<-|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ then that first coordinate is negative. In
particular $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ maps the future open cone
$\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ into itself.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with the following data. In this notation $V$ includes its
specified orientation; forgetting that orientation gives only the underlying
real vector space, not the full datum $V$ of the model.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space with
the smooth structure of [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]], and
let $p\in A$. A smooth germ at $p$ is the equivalence class of a smooth real function on an
open neighbourhood of $p$, where representatives agreeing on a smaller
neighbourhood are equivalent ([[def-germ-of-a-smooth-function-at-a-point]]).
For such a germ $[f]$ define

$$\Phi_p(v)([f]):=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}f(p+tv),\qquad v\in V .$$

Then $\Phi_p:V\to T_pA$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$ onto the tangent space
$T_pA$; in particular $T_pA$ is canonically identified with $V$, independently
of any chart. If $x$ is an inertial chart and
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$, then the coordinate derivations satisfy
$\Phi_p(v)=\sum_av^a\partial_a|_p$.

Let $B$ be a Hamel basis of a vector space $V$. For each $b\in B$, the **coordinate functional** $b^*:V\to F$ is defined by

$$b^*(c)=\delta_{bc}\qquad(c\in B),$$

and extended linearly: if the unique finite basis expansion of $v$ is $v=\sum_{c\in S}a_cc$, then $b^*(v)=a_b$, with $a_b:=0$ when $b\notin S$. Uniqueness of finite basis expansions makes this single-valued, and coordinatewise addition and scalar multiplication make $b^*$ linear. The family $(b^*)_{b\in B}$ is the **dual family associated to $B$**.

When $B$ is finite this family is the usual dual basis. When $B$ is infinite it remains a family in $V^*$, but it need not span the whole algebraic dual.

derivations.claim: Write the transition as $x'^a=\Lambda^a{}_cx^c+b^a$ with $\Lambda$ invertible, $\det\Lambda=+1$ and $\Lambda$ orthochronous by [L1] and [L2]; the inverse relation is $x^c=(\Lambda^{-1})^c{}_a(x'^a-b^a)$. At a point where the scalar coordinate representation is totally differentiable, the affine coordinate maps are differentiable, so the total chain rule [L12] gives $\partial_c=\frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^c}\partial'_a=\Lambda^a{}_c\partial'_a$ and $\partial'_a=\frac{\partial x^c}{\partial x'^a}\partial_c=(\Lambda^{-1})^c{}_a\partial_c$, and the two matrices are inverse: $\Lambda^a{}_c(\Lambda^{-1})^c{}_d=\delta^a_d$ and $(\Lambda^{-1})^c{}_a\Lambda^a{}_d=\delta^c_d$ by [L12].

For (vii), let $U$ be $\mathcal C^1$ future timelike and $\rho_0$ a $\mathcal C^1$ scalar; then $J=\rho_0U$ has components $J^a=\rho_0U^a$ and is $\mathcal C^1$ by the product rule of [L12]. In an inertial chart the future timelike vectors are the coordinate set $C^+=\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ by [L11] and [L9], so $U^0>0$ and $u:=U/U^0$ is well defined with $u^0=1$ and $u^i=U^i/U^0$; moreover $\rho:=J^0=\rho_0U^0$ and $J=\rho_0U=\rho_0U^0(U/U^0)=\rho u$. Since $\rho-\rho_0=\rho_0(U^0-1)$, one has $\rho=\rho_0$ exactly when $\rho_0(U^0-1)=0$, and when $\rho_0\neq0$ this is equivalent to $U^0=1$. The vector $u$ has first component $1$ but is not asserted to satisfy any unit or four-velocity normalization; with the convention $x^0=ct$ of [L9], a curve whose coordinate tangent is proportional to $U$ has $\mathrm dx^i/\mathrm dt=c\,U^i/U^0=cu^i$. No identification of $J$ with a physical current is made: the Interpretation boundary of the Statement records that this requires a model premise. This proves (vii).

For the vector field, [L3] and [L4] write $J=J^c\partial_c$ in the chart $x$ and $J=J'^a\partial'_a$ in the chart $x'$; substituting $\partial_c=\Lambda^a{}_c\partial'_a$ from step 1.1 gives $J=J^c\Lambda^a{}_c\partial'_a$, and comparing coefficients in the basis $(\partial'_a)$ of the tangent space gives $J'^a=\Lambda^a{}_cJ^c$; this proves (i).

For the covector field, write $k=k_b\,dx^b$ and $k=k'_a\,dx'^a$; since $x^c=(\Lambda^{-1})^c{}_a(x'^a-b^a)$, the chain rule [L12] gives $dx^c=(\Lambda^{-1})^c{}_a\,dx'^a$, so $k=k_b(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_a\,dx'^a$ and comparing coefficients gives $k'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_ak_b$. For the phase function, substitute the inverse relation: $k_ax^a+\theta_0=k_a(\Lambda^{-1})^a{}_c(x'^c-b^c)+\theta_0=k'_cx'^c+\theta_0-k'_cb^c$, where the last step uses $k'_c=k_a(\Lambda^{-1})^a{}_c$; hence $\theta=k'_ax'^a+\theta'_0$ with $\theta'_0=\theta_0-k'_ab^a$, and the phase function has the same value at every event in both charts. This proves (ii).

For the tensor law, [L1] gives $e'_a=Le_a$ with $L$ proper orthochronous and matrix $M$ satisfying $e'_a=M^b{}_ae_b$ with $M=\Lambda^{-1}$; consequently the dual bases satisfy $e'^{*a}=\Lambda^a{}_be^{*b}$ (both sides pair with $e'_c=\sum_b(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_ce_b$ to give $\delta^a_c$ by [L4] and the inverse relations of step 1.1). By the component definition of [L3] and multilinearity of $T(p)$, $T'^{a_1\dots a_r}{}_{b_1\dots b_s}=T(p)(e'^{*a_1},\dots,e'_{b_1},\dots)=\Lambda^{a_1}{}_{c_1}\cdots(\Lambda^{-1})^{d_1}{}_{b_1}\cdots T^{c_1\dots c_r}{}_{d_1\dots d_s}$, which is the displayed law. Contracting the first contravariant with the first covariant index in the transformed components gives $\Lambda^{a}{}_{c}(\Lambda^{-1})^{d}{}_{a}\cdots=\delta^d{}_c\cdots$, which is the contraction of the untransformed components; the remaining free indices retain their respective transformation factors, yielding precisely the component law of the same type-$(r-1,s-1)$ tensor $\operatorname{ctr}(T)$. Thus contraction is invariant as an intrinsic operation, as [L5] states; a fully contracted scalar has the same numerical value in both charts. For the metric, its components are $\eta_{ab}=\eta(e_a,e_b)$ in any frame, and by [L2] and [L1] $\eta'_{ab}=\eta(e'_a,e'_b)=\eta(Le_a,Le_b)=\eta(e_a,e_b)=\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ in every inertial frame. This proves (iii).

At an event where all coordinate components of $J$ are totally differentiable, linear combinations and affine precomposition preserve total differentiability by [L12]; this is automatic for $\ell\ge1$ and is the additional pointwise hypothesis for $\ell=0$. For the derivative law on a totally differentiable scalar, step 1.1 gives $\partial'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_a\partial_b$. For the divergence, (i) gives $J'^a=\Lambda^a{}_cJ^c$, so $\partial'_aJ'^a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_a\partial_b(\Lambda^a{}_cJ^c)=\delta^b{}_c\partial_bJ^c=\partial_aJ^a$, using the inverse relations of step 1.1 and the index rule of [L12]. For a $C^1$ type-$(2,0)$ field all components are totally differentiable; (iii) gives $T'^{ab}=\Lambda^a{}_c\Lambda^b{}_dT^{cd}$, hence $\partial'_aT'^{ab}=(\Lambda^{-1})^e{}_a\partial_e(\Lambda^a{}_c\Lambda^b{}_dT^{cd})=\delta^e{}_c\Lambda^b{}_d\partial_eT^{cd}=\Lambda^b{}_d\partial_aT^{ad}$. This proves (iv).

An alternating covariant tensor field is a covariant tensor field by [L6], so the covariant law of (iii) applies on each slot and no further structure is involved. For the oriented volume form, its components in the two frames are $\epsilon_{abcd}=\epsilon(e_a,e_b,e_c,e_d)$ and $\epsilon'_{abcd}=\epsilon(e'_a,e'_b,e'_c,e'_d)$ by [L6]; since $e'_a=Le_a$ with $L$ proper by [L1], [L7] gives $\epsilon'_{abcd}=\epsilon(Le_a,Le_b,Le_c,Le_d)=\det(L)\,\epsilon(e_a,e_b,e_c,e_d)=\epsilon_{abcd}$, while for $\det L=-1$ the same computation gives the opposite sign. This proves (v).

For $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf0$, [L8] gives $J'=J$ directly; the spatial correction in (vi) is zero by that convention. For nonzero $\boldsymbol\beta$, clause (vi) is the special case of (i) and (iv) for the passive boost: the continuity equation is the component expansion $\partial_aJ^a=\partial_0J^0+\sum_i\partial_iJ^i$, and substituting $\Lambda=B(\boldsymbol\beta)$, $\Lambda^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ into $J'^a=\Lambda^a{}_bJ^b$ and reading the matrix entries of [L8] gives $J'^0=\gamma(J^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot J_{\mathrm{cov}})$ and $J'_{\mathrm{cov}}=J_{\mathrm{cov}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot J_{\mathrm{cov}})\boldsymbol\beta-\gamma\boldsymbol\beta J^0$.

Clause (i) is step 2.1, clause (ii) is step 2.2, clause (iii) is step 2.3, clause (iv) is step 3.1, clause (v) is step 3.2, clause (vi) is step 4.1 and clause (vii) is step 1.2; the Interpretation boundary is a restriction on the reading of the components and is not used as a premise anywhere. This proves every clause of the statement.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement quantifies over open $\Omega\subseteq A$ and tensor fields of every type; the zero field is an instance, so the scoped class is nonempty.
Steps 1.1-1.2 and 2.1-2.2 include the zero vector and covector components and the zero tensor field; the continuity equation is checked as an identity.
Proof 2.1 and 2.2 give the single-index vector and covector laws; Proof 3.1 gives divergence and the remaining contravariant factor for type (2,0).

Proof 2.3 proves contraction as an intrinsic operation with the remaining free-index factors retained, and preserves the metric components. Proof 3.2 treats alternating fields; repeated indices vanish only for alternating tensors.
The chart indices range over the finite endpoint values $0$ and $3$; step 1.2 and step 4.1 verify the component laws for every index including those endpoints.

The same sum in Proof 4.1 supplies the reverse continuity-equation equivalence; applying the inverse coordinate relation in Proof 2.2 recovers the original phase and constant term.

risk_review.notes: All nine steps checked: components compare one event; basis M=Lambda^{-1} and dual Lambda give the variance-slot laws. Contraction cancels paired factors while free indices still transform; complete contractions alone are scalar numerical invariants. Total differentiability is required for derivatives at ell=0; ell≥1 guarantees it. Constant Lambda cancels in divergence and leaves the free Lambda on rank-two divergence. Zero boost uses identity. Arbitrary rho0, including zero/negative, obeys rho=rho0 U0 and equality iff rho0(U0-1)=0. Replacing [L1] with these exact directions reconciles it with Proof 2.3. Statement and proof unchanged; this is a facts-only correction.

boundaries.reason: The remark records reconstruction obligations for verbal postulate systems; it asserts no existence or non-existence of a set of models.
No zero parameter, zero vector or degenerate limit occurs in the remark.
The remark introduces no indexed family whose length-one case could be special.
The remark lists assumptions and open obligations; there is no algebraic or geometric degenerate case to dispose of.
The remark contains no interval, boundary or limiting endpoint.
The remark performs no selection and invokes no choice principle.
The remark deliberately does not assert the equivalence of the verbal axiom systems of the literature; it records that equivalence as an open obligation.
For the same reason the remark asserts no converse equivalence; the reconstruction program is listed, not carried out.

citations.quote:
Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be its coordinates, so that a vector is written
$x=x^0e_0+x^1e_1+x^2e_2+x^3e_3$ and the spatial part is the coordinate
column $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ with its standard
Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

For $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$, where
$|\boldsymbol\beta|$ is the Euclidean norm, set

$$\gamma(\boldsymbol\beta):=(1-|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)^{-1/2}\ \ge 1,$$

with equality exactly for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ and strict inequality
for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$; here the power is the rational power
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). The **passive Lorentz
boost with parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$** is the linear map
$B(\boldsymbol\beta):V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) defined by its action on
coordinates: for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$,

$$x'^0=\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}),\qquad x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\,(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})\,\boldsymbol\beta-\gamma\,\boldsymbol\beta\,x^0,$$

and for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$, $B(\mathbf 0):=\operatorname{id}_V$.
Here $x'$ denotes the coordinates of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ applied to the
vector with coordinates $x$, and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is
the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the matrix of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}\gamma & -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta & I_3+\dfrac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\,\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix},$$

that is, $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ for
$i=1,2,3$, and
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$
for $i,j=1,2,3$, with the spatial block replaced by
$I_3$ when $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$. In the $1+1$ case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\beta e_1$ this reads
$x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$ and $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$. The vector
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is called the **boost parameter**; it is dimensionless and
mathematically independent of any unit convention.

**Consistency of the definition.** The displayed formulas assign to every
coordinate pair $(x^0,x_{\mathrm{vec}})$ a pair
$(x'^0,x'_{\mathrm{vec}})$; writing the result as the matrix product above and
using that $\mathbb R^4$ is identified with coordinates through
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] (see
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), the map
$v\mapsto E(M(E^{-1}(v)))$ is the unique linear map with that matrix. The case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ is declared separately because the expression
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ is undefined there. That the two cases fit
together is the limit computation recorded next.

**The limit as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$.** For
$\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$ the identity
$\gamma^2-1=|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\gamma^2$ gives

$$\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\gamma+1}.$$

Since $|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\le3/4$ forces $1\le\gamma\le2$, the bounds
$|\beta_i|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|$ and $|\beta_i\beta_j|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$
(from the Euclidean norm convention, [[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]])
show that $\gamma\to1$ as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$; here continuity of
the positive-base power at fixed exponent $-1/2$ is
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], with real and rational powers
identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. Hence
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\to1/2$, so
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac12\beta_i\beta_j+o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)\to I$ entrywise, without a hidden division by zero.
Here $o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ denotes a remainder whose ratio to
$|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ tends to $0$ through nonzero parameters: the ratio
of each spatial remainder is bounded by
$|\gamma^2/(\gamma+1)-1/2|\to0$. The time-space entries obey
$|\gamma\beta_i|\le2|\boldsymbol\beta|\to0$, and the time-time entry tends to
$1$ by $\gamma\to1$. The
definition asserts no Lorentz property: that $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ is proved in
[[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], and its collinear
composition law in
[[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]. The physical
reading of $c\boldsymbol\beta$ as a relative velocity is not part of this
definition ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

Let $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ be the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] in an
inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. For every
$\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the following
hold.

(i) $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map:
$\eta(B(\boldsymbol\beta)v,B(\boldsymbol\beta)w)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$,
$\det B(\boldsymbol\beta)=+1$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)(C^+)=C^+$.

(ii) $B(\mathbf 0)$ is the identity, and for every $\boldsymbol\beta$ the image
of the frame vector $e_0$ is
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)e_0=\gamma\,(e_0-\beta_1e_1-\beta_2e_2-\beta_3e_3)$, so
the map $\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is injective and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ fixes $0_V$; moreover every vector $y$ with
coordinates $(0,y_{\mathrm{vec}})$ and
$\boldsymbol\beta\cdot y_{\mathrm{vec}}=0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)y=y$.

(iii) $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)B(\boldsymbol\beta)
=B(\boldsymbol\beta)B(-\boldsymbol\beta)=\operatorname{id}_V$; in particular
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is invertible with
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and
$B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ are inverse bijections of $V$.

(iv) If $u$ is a future timelike unit vector with coordinates
$(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$, so that $\eta(u,u)=-1$, $u^0>0$ and
$|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|<u^0$, then the boost with parameter
$\boldsymbol\beta:=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)u=e_0$.

(v) If a vector $x$ has $x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$, then the first coordinate of
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)x$ is $\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})>0$;
if $x^0<-|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ then that first coordinate is negative. In
particular $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ maps the future open cone
$\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ into itself.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ be the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] in an
inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. For every
$\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the following
hold.

(i) $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map:
$\eta(B(\boldsymbol\beta)v,B(\boldsymbol\beta)w)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$,
$\det B(\boldsymbol\beta)=+1$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)(C^+)=C^+$.

(ii) $B(\mathbf 0)$ is the identity, and for every $\boldsymbol\beta$ the image
of the frame vector $e_0$ is
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)e_0=\gamma\,(e_0-\beta_1e_1-\beta_2e_2-\beta_3e_3)$, so
the map $\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is injective and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ fixes $0_V$; moreover every vector $y$ with
coordinates $(0,y_{\mathrm{vec}})$ and
$\boldsymbol\beta\cdot y_{\mathrm{vec}}=0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)y=y$.

(iii) $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)B(\boldsymbol\beta)
=B(\boldsymbol\beta)B(-\boldsymbol\beta)=\operatorname{id}_V$; in particular
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is invertible with
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and
$B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ are inverse bijections of $V$.

(iv) If $u$ is a future timelike unit vector with coordinates
$(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$, so that $\eta(u,u)=-1$, $u^0>0$ and
$|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|<u^0$, then the boost with parameter
$\boldsymbol\beta:=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)u=e_0$.

(v) If a vector $x$ has $x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$, then the first coordinate of
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)x$ is $\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})>0$;
if $x^0<-|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ then that first coordinate is negative. In
particular $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ maps the future open cone
$\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ into itself.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

derivations.claim: Evaluate the $2\times2$ matrix $B$: $\gamma=(1-9/25)^{-1/2}=(16/25)^{-1/2}=5/4$, so $B=\begin{pmatrix}5/4&-3/4\\ -3/4&5/4\end{pmatrix}$, and $B$ acts as the identity on the coordinate directions $e_2,e_3$ because $\boldsymbol\beta=3/5\,e_1$ has vanishing $e_2,e_3$ components in [L1]. For the product $B^{T}\eta_0B$, the four entries are $(5/4)(-5/4)+(-3/4)(-3/4)=-25/16+9/16=-1$ in the $(0,0)$ slot, $(5/4)(3/4)+(-3/4)(5/4)=15/16-15/16=0$ and $(-3/4)(-5/4)+(5/4)(-3/4)=15/16-15/16=0$ in the two off-diagonal slots, and $(-3/4)(3/4)+(5/4)(5/4)=-9/16+25/16=1$ in the $(1,1)$ slot; hence $B^{T}\eta_0B=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)=\eta_0$.
The determinant is $\det B=(5/4)(5/4)-(-3/4)(-3/4)=25/16-9/16=1$, so $B$ is proper in the sense of the properness condition of [L2].

By [L2], $Be_0=\gamma(e_0-\beta e_1)=(5/4)(e_0-(3/5)e_1)$, with coordinates $(5/4,-3/4)$; [L3] gives $\eta(Be_0,Be_0)=-(5/4)^2+(3/4)^2=-1$, so $Be_0$ is timelike by [L5]. Since $B$ is orthochronous by [L2] and $e_0\in C^+$ by [L3], [L4] gives $Be_0\in B(C^+)=C^+$, so $Be_0$ is future timelike: the future timelike vector $e_0$ is mapped to a future timelike vector.

The product of clause (iv) is $\begin{pmatrix}5/4&3/4\\ 3/4&5/4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}5/4&-3/4\\ -3/4&5/4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}25/16-9/16&-15/16+15/16\\ -15/16+15/16&-9/16+25/16\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}$, and the first factor is the matrix of $B(-3/5)$ by [L1]; this is the instance at $\beta=3/5$ of $B(-\beta)B(\beta)=\operatorname{id}$ from [L2], so the inverse is the boost with the opposite parameter.

For the two null directions, [L1] gives $B(1,1)=\bigl((5/4)(1-3/5),(5/4)(1-3/5)\bigr)=(1/2,1/2)$ and $B(1,-1)=\bigl((5/4)(1+3/5),(5/4)(-1-3/5)\bigr)=(2,-2)$; both images satisfy $\eta_0=0$ on their squares: $-(1/2)^2+(1/2)^2=0$ and $-4+4=0$, so they are null by [L5]. Since $B(1,1)=\tfrac12(1,1)$ and $B(1,-1)=2(1,-1)$, the image of the line $x^1=x^0$ is the same line and the image of the line $x^1=-x^0$ is the same line; hence the pair of null lines $\{x^1=x^0\}\cup\{x^1=-x^0\}$ is mapped onto itself, and the images are exactly that pair.

For the event with coordinates $(13,11)$, [L1] gives $x'^0=(5/4)(13-(3/5)11)=(5/4)(13-33/5)=(5/4)(32/5)=8$ and $x'^1=(5/4)(11-(3/5)13)=(5/4)(11-39/5)=(5/4)(16/5)=4$, while $(0,0)$ is fixed because the boost is linear. The interval in $\eta_0$ is $-(8)^2+(4)^2=-64+16=-48$ and $-(13)^2+(11)^2=-169+121=-48$; this numerical equality is the instance of $B^{T}\eta_0B=\eta_0$ from step 1.1 applied to the coordinate difference $(13,11)$.
